name: Hadwiger's Conjecture
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: For a finite simple graph G, a minor of G is any graph obtainable by deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges; the Hadwiger number h(G) is the largest t for which the complete graph K_t is a minor of G. A proper colouring assigns colours to vertices so that adjacent vertices differ, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours in a proper colouring. Hadwiger's conjecture asserts that for every r ∈ ℕ and every finite simple graph G, r ≤ χ(G) implies r ≤ h(G): a graph that needs at least r colours must contain K_r as a minor. Equivalently — the form stated here — every graph with no K_(r+1) minor (i.e. h(G) ≤ r) is (r+1)-colourable. The case r = 4 is equivalent to the Four-Colour Theorem, and Robertson, Seymour and Thomas settled r = 5; the conjecture is open for all r ≥ 6.
formal_statement: theorem P001 : ¬ ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), HadwigerConj G

name: Excluded Minors of GF(pᵐ)-Representable Matroids (universal)
msc: 05B35 Combinatorial aspects of matroids and geometric lattices
informal_statement_summary: A matroid M = (E, I) consists of a finite ground set E and a family I of independent subsets such that ∅ is independent, subsets of independent sets are independent, and the exchange axiom holds (if I, J ∈ I with |I| < |J| then I ∪ {x} ∈ I for some x ∈ J \ I). For a prime p and integer m ≥ 1, M is GF(pᵐ)-representable if its independent sets are exactly the linearly independent column-sets of some matrix over the finite field GF(pᵐ). Minors are formed by deletion and contraction; a minor is proper if it differs from M. The class of GF(pᵐ)-representable matroids is closed under minors, so it is characterised by its excluded minors — the matroids outside the class all of whose proper minors lie in it. By the Geelen–Gerards–Whittle theorem (formerly Rota's conjecture) this list is finite for every prime power. The challenge: for every r that is a prime power pᵐ, show that a complete finite list L of these excluded minors exists — pairwise non-isomorphic, with every non-representable matroid having a minor isomorphic to a member of L. This is Rota's conjecture itself (the formal statement cannot demand that L be given explicitly); its proof by Geelen, Gerards and Whittle has been announced but not published in full, so the problem is filed as a research result. Known lists: U₂,₄ for GF(2) (Tutte); U₂,₅, U₃,₅, F₇, F₇* for GF(3) (Bixby, Seymour); and the GF(4) list (Geelen, Gerards, Kapoor).
formal_statement: theorem P002 (r p m : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hm : 0 < m) (hr : r = p ^ m) : RotaConj p m

name: Caccetta–Häggkvist Conjecture (universal)
msc: 05C20 Directed graphs (digraphs), tournaments; 05C38 Paths and cycles
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 3: The Caccetta--H\"aggkvist Conjecture}
\refstepcounter{section}

\begin{definition}[Digraphs, out-degree, directed cycles]
A \emph{digraph} $D$ on a finite vertex set $V$ consists of a set $A\subseteq V\times V$ of \emph{arcs}; loops $(v,v)$ are allowed. The \emph{out-degree} $d^+(v)$ of a vertex $v$ is the number of arcs $(v,w)\in A$, and $\delta^+(D)=\min_{v\in V} d^+(v)$ is the \emph{minimum out-degree} of $D$. A \emph{directed cycle of length $k\ge 1$} is a sequence $v_0,\dots,v_{k-1}$ of $k$ distinct vertices with $(v_i,v_{i+1})\in A$ for all $i$, indices taken modulo $k$; thus a loop is a directed cycle of length $1$ and a pair of opposite arcs is one of length $2$.
\end{definition}

For $n>r\ge 1$ the circulant digraph on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with arcs $i\to i+1,\dots,i\to i+r$ has minimum out-degree $r$, and its shortest directed cycle has length exactly $\lceil n/r\rceil$. Caccetta and H\"aggkvist \cite{caccetta1978minimal} conjectured in 1978 that no digraph of minimum out-degree $r$ does better.

\begin{openproblem}[Scaled Caccetta--H\"aggkvist problem]
Let $r\in\N$ with $r\ge 1$. Prove that every digraph on $n$ vertices with minimum out-degree at least $r$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$.
\end{openproblem}

The case $r=1$ is immediate (follow out-arcs until a vertex repeats). Caccetta and H\"aggkvist \cite{caccetta1978minimal} proved the case $r=2$, Hamidoune \cite{hamidoune1987note} the case $r=3$, and Ho\`ang and Reed \cite{hoang1987note} the cases $r=4$ and $r=5$. The problem is open from $r=6$ onwards. The conjecture is also known when $r$ is small compared with $n$: Shen proved it whenever $r\le\sqrt{n/2}$ (see the survey \cite{sullivan2006summary}). In general only approximate versions are available. Chv\'atal and Szemer\'edi \cite{chvatal1983short} showed that minimum out-degree $r$ forces a directed cycle of length at most $2n/r$, and one of length at most $n/r+2500$; the additive constant was lowered to $304$ by Nishimura \cite{nishimura1988short} and to $73$ by Shen \cite{shen2002caccetta}. The most studied special case is $r=\lceil n/3\rceil$, which asks for a directed cycle of length at most $3$; it is known for minimum out-degree at least $0.3532n$ \cite{hamburger2007directed} and $0.3465n$ \cite{hladky2017counting}, and remains open at $n/3$.

Two related conjectures are worth recording. The conjecture of Behzad, Chartrand and Wall \cite{behzad1970minimal} is the special case of $r$-regular digraphs. The conjecture of Ho\`ang and Reed \cite{hoang1987note}---every digraph with minimum out-degree $r$ contains directed cycles $C_1,\dots,C_r$ such that each $C_j$ meets $C_1\cup\dots\cup C_{j-1}$ in at most one vertex---implies the Caccetta--H\"aggkvist conjecture.

informal_statement_summary: A digraph on a finite vertex set is a set of ordered pairs of vertices (arcs); loops are allowed. The out-degree of a vertex is the number of arcs leaving it, and a directed cycle of length k ≥ 1 is a sequence of k distinct vertices each joined by an arc to the cyclically next one. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture (1978) states that for every r ≥ 1, every digraph on n vertices in which every vertex has out-degree at least r contains a directed cycle of length at most ⌈n/r⌉; the circulant digraph on Z_n with arcs i → i+1, …, i → i+r shows that the bound cannot be improved. The scaled problem asks, for a given r ≥ 1, for a proof of the conjecture at that r. The cases r ≤ 5 are known (Caccetta–Häggkvist for r = 2, Hamidoune for r = 3, Hoàng–Reed for r = 4, 5), as is the regime r ≤ √(n/2) (Shen); the problem is open from r = 6 onwards, and even the directed-triangle case r = ⌈n/3⌉ is open. The universal version asserts the conjecture for every r ≥ 1.
formal_statement: theorem P003 : CaccettaHaggkvistConj

name: Sidorenko's Conjecture for Bipartite Graphs with Bounded Sides (universal)
msc: 05C35 Extremal problems in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: For simple graphs H and G, a graph homomorphism H → G is a vertex map sending every edge of H to an edge of G; writing hom(H, G) for the number of such maps, the homomorphism density of H in G is t_H(G) = hom(H, G) / |V(G)|^|V(H)|. Sidorenko's conjecture states that for every bipartite graph H and every graph G, t_H(G) ≥ t_{K₂}(G)^|E(H)| — the edge density of G raised to the number of edges of H. Since the conjecture is open in general, this challenge poses a scalable weakening that bounds the two sides of the bipartition: for a parameter r, restrict to bipartite graphs H admitting a bipartition V(H) = X ∪ Y with |X| ≤ r and |Y| ≤ r. As r → ∞ this class exhausts all bipartite graphs, so the family interpolates between small, tractable cases and the full conjecture; the universal version asks for a proof or disproof for every r. (The specific instance of the half-graph H_r is split off as a separate problem.)
formal_statement: theorem P004 : ¬ ∀ (W V : Type) [Fintype W] [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] (H : SimpleGraph W) (G : SimpleGraph V), SidorenkoConj H G

name: Erdős–Hajnal Conjecture for Paths (universal)
msc: 05C55 Generalized Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: In a simple graph, a clique is a set of pairwise-adjacent vertices and an independent set is a set of pairwise-non-adjacent vertices, and G is H-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to H. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture states that for each graph H there is a constant c_H > 0 such that every H-free graph on n vertices contains a clique or independent set of size at least n^(c_H) — a polynomial guarantee, far larger than the logarithmic size forced in general graphs. This challenge is the parametrized case H = P_r, the path on r vertices: for every r there is a constant c_r > 0 such that every P_r-free finite graph G has a clique or independent set of size at least |V(G)|^(c_r). The case r = 5 has recently been resolved (Nguyen, Scott and Seymour).
formal_statement: theorem P005 : EHforPaths

name: Better-Quasi-Ordering of Finite Graphs under Minors (universal)
msc: 05C83 Graph minors
informal_statement_summary: A quasi-order (Q, ≤) is well-quasi-ordered (a wqo) if it has no infinite strictly descending chain and no infinite antichain. Better-quasi-order (bqo) is a strengthening of wqo, due to Nash-Williams, that — unlike wqo — is preserved under forming transfinite iterated power-sets; (Q, ≤) is bqo precisely when it is α-well-quasi-ordered for every ordinal α (in particular for ω₁). Robertson and Seymour famously proved that finite graphs are well-quasi-ordered under the minor relation (every infinite family of graphs has one that is a minor of another). This challenge is the conjectured strengthening in ordinal-indexed form: for every ordinal r, the finite simple graphs (odd r) or the finite planar graphs (even r) are ⌊r/2⌋-well-quasi-ordered under the minor relation; over all r this says that finite graphs are better-quasi-ordered under minors.
formal_statement: theorem P006 : GraphMinorWQOConj

name: Sphere Packing Problem (universal)
msc: 52C17 Packing and covering in n dimensions
informal_statement_summary: In dimension d, a unit packing is a set of centres pairwise at distance ≥ 2 (so the unit balls around them do not overlap); its upper density is the limsup as R → ∞ of the fraction of the ball B(0, R) covered by those unit balls, and the sphere-packing constant Δ_d is the supremum of densities over all unit packings. The sphere-packing problem asks for Δ_d; the value is known only for d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 8, 24} (d = 3 is the Kepler conjecture; d = 8 and d = 24 are Viazovska and Cohn–Kumar–Miller–Radchenko–Viazovska), the largest solved case being d = 24, and in each the optimum is attained by a lattice (ℤ, A₂, the FCC lattice, E₈, the Leech lattice). The universal challenge asks whether the optimum is always attained by a lattice (Δ_d = Δ_d^L) — open in general and widely expected to fail in high dimensions.
formal_statement: theorem P007 : LatticeOptimalConj

name: Ryser's Hypergraph Conjecture (universal)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 8: Ryser's Hypergraph Conjecture}
\refstepcounter{section}



\begin{definition}[$r$-partite]
Given $r\in \mathbb{N}$, an $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ is \emph{$r$-partite} if there is a partition
$$
V\ev{\mathcal{H}} = \bigcup_{i=1}^{r} P_i
$$
of the vertex set of $\mathcal{H}$ such that $|P_i \cap e| = 1$, for each $e\in E\ev{\mathcal{H}}$ and $i\in [r]$. 
\end{definition}


\begin{definition}[Cover number]
Given a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, a
set $C$ of vertices of $\mathcal{H}$ is a \textit{vertex cover} if it contains a vertex of every edge. The smallest cardinality of a vertex cover of $\mathcal{H}$ is called the \textit{cover number} of $\mathcal{H}$. It is denoted by $\tau(\mathcal{H})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Matching number]
The \textit{matching number} of a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ is the largest cardinality of a set of pairwise disjoint edges of $\mathcal{H}$. It is denoted by $\nu\ev{\mathcal{H}}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{conjecture}[Ryser's Conjecture \mbox{\cite{bishnoi}}]
Let $r\in \mathbb{N}$.
Every $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ satisfies:
$$
\tau\ev{\mathcal{H}} \leq \ev{r-1} \cdot \nu\ev{\mathcal{H}}
$$

\end{conjecture}

\paragraph{Status (October 2026).} Ryser's conjecture was disproved in OpenAI's math release (\texttt{github.com/openai/math}; Lean proof checked by Comparator, not yet independently verified). The formal challenge therefore asks for a proof of the \emph{negation} of the universal statement above.

For $r=2$, it is a classical theorem of K\H{o}nig, and for $r=3$ it was proved by Aharoni \cite{AharoniRyserTripartite} using the topological method.

\paragraph{Formalisation notes.} The formal statement quantifies over $r \geq 2$. A hypergraph has a finite vertex set and a set of edges, each a subset of the vertex set (so there are no repeated edges). The cover number is defined as the infimum of the sizes of vertex covers, with value $0$ when no vertex cover exists; this happens only when some edge is empty, which is impossible in an $r$-partite hypergraph with $r \geq 1$, so the convention plays no role here. The matching number is the largest size of a matching, which exists because there are finitely many matchings.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{thebibliography}{2}
\bibitem{bishnoi} Anurag Bishnoi, Shagnik Das, Patrick Morris, Tibor Szabó. \emph{Ryser's Conjecture for $t$-intersecting hypergraphs}. (2020). arXiv:2001.04132.
\bibitem{AharoniRyserTripartite} Aharoni, Ron. \emph{Ryser's conjecture for tripartite 3-graphs}. Combinatorica \textbf{21}(1), 1--4. (2001). \texttt{doi:10.1007/s004930170001}.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: A hypergraph is r-uniform if every edge has exactly r vertices, and r-partite if its vertex set can be partitioned into r classes P₁,…,P_r meeting each edge in exactly one vertex of each class. A vertex cover is a set of vertices meeting every edge, and the cover number τ(H) is the least size of a vertex cover; the matching number ν(H) is the greatest number of pairwise-disjoint edges. Ryser's conjecture states that every r-partite r-uniform hypergraph H satisfies τ(H) ≤ (r − 1)·ν(H). For r = 2 this is König's theorem; r = 3 was proved by Aharoni via a topological method; it was open for all r ≥ 4 until October 2026, when OpenAI's math release gave counterexamples (not yet independently verified); the formal challenge asks for a proof of the negation.
formal_statement: theorem P008 : ¬ RyserConjecture.{u}

name: Union-Closed Sets Conjecture (universal)
msc: 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: A finite family F of finite sets is union-closed if A ∪ B ∈ F whenever A, B ∈ F, and the density of an element x is the fraction |{F ∈ F : x ∈ F}| / |F| of members containing x. Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture asserts that every finite union-closed family other than {∅} and the empty family has an element of density at least 1/2. The scaled version asks, for every r, for an element of density at least 1/2 − 1/(r+2); the formal challenge is the full conjecture with density 1/2. The entropy method gives an unconditional density of about 0.382, which settles the small cases; the conjecture is open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P009 : UnionClosedConj F

name: Unfriendly Partition Conjecture (universal)
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A partition of the vertices of a graph into two classes is unfriendly if every vertex has at least as many neighbours in the opposite class as in its own. The unfriendly partition conjecture asks whether every countable graph has an unfriendly partition; this can fail for some uncountable graphs and is open for countable ones. This challenge is the countable conjecture itself, with neighbourhood cardinalities compared by injections so that vertices of infinite degree are handled correctly. The source document also poses a transfinite scaled version via an ordinal-bounded 'r-partitioning game' between a Challenger and a Partitioner, conjecturing that the Partitioner always wins on a countable graph.
formal_statement: theorem P010 : UPConj G

name: Vizing's Theorem (edge chromatic number ≤ Δ + 1)
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: Let G be a finite graph. A proper edge-colouring of G assigns a colour to each edge so that any two edges sharing a common endpoint receive different colours, and the edge chromatic number χ′(G) is the least number of colours for which a proper edge-colouring exists. Let Δ(G), the maximum degree of G, be the largest number of edges incident with any single vertex. Vizing's theorem states that these two parameters differ by at most one: every finite graph satisfies Δ(G) ≤ χ′(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1. The lower bound Δ(G) ≤ χ′(G) is immediate, since the Δ(G) edges at a maximum-degree vertex must all receive distinct colours; the content of the theorem is the upper bound χ′(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1.
formal_statement: theorem P011 [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] : edgeChromaticNumber G ≤ G.maxDegree + 1

name: Koksma's Lower Bound for Partial Transversals of Latin Squares
msc: 05B15 Orthogonal arrays, Latin squares, Room squares
informal_statement_summary: Let S be a finite set with |S| = n. A latin square on S is a matrix M : S × S → S, with rows and columns both indexed by S and entries in S, in which no symbol is repeated within any row or any column; equivalently, for every column c the map r ↦ M(r, c) is injective, and for every row r the map c ↦ M(r, c) is injective. The number n is the size of M. A partial transversal of M is a set T ⊆ S × S of cells that lie in pairwise distinct rows, lie in pairwise distinct columns, and carry pairwise distinct symbols — formally, the projections (r, c) ↦ r and (r, c) ↦ c are each injective on T, and (r, c) ↦ M(r, c) is injective on T. Koksma's theorem states that every latin square of size n ≥ 7 has a partial transversal of size at least (2n + 1)/3, i.e. of size T with 3T ≥ 2n + 1.
formal_statement: theorem P012 {hM : IsLatinSq M} {hN : Fintype.card S ≥ 7} : ∃ pt, IsPT M pt ∧ 3 * #pt ≥ 2 * (Fintype.card S) + 1

name: Beck–Fiala discrepancy theorem
msc: 05D05 Extremal set theory; 11K38 Discrepancy and irregularities of distribution
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 13: The Beck--Fiala Discrepancy Theorem}

Let $V$ and $I$ be finite sets, and let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be an indexed family
of subsets of $V$. Repeated sets are allowed and counted separately.
The degree of a point $v$ is $|\{i\in I:v\in A_i\}|$.
A signing is a function $\chi:V\to\{-1,1\}$; its discrepancy on $A_i$ is
$\left|\sum_{v\in A_i}\chi(v)\right|$.

\begin{theorem}[Beck--Fiala \cite{BeckFiala1981}]
Let $t\geq 1$ be an integer. If every point has degree at most $t$, then
there is a signing $\chi$ such that, for every $i\in I$,
\[
\left|\sum_{v\in A_i}\chi(v)\right|\leq 2t-1.
\]
\end{theorem}

This is the classical linear discrepancy bound, not the open Beck--Fiala
conjecture asking for a bound of order $\sqrt{t}$.
Empty ground sets, empty families and empty member sets are allowed.

\paragraph{A consequence.}
If every $A_i$ has size at least $2t$, the discrepancy bound implies
that every $A_i$ contains points of both signs, so such a set system
has property B.

\begin{thebibliography}{1}
\bibitem{BeckFiala1981}
J.~Beck and T.~Fiala, ``Integer-making'' theorems,
\emph{Discrete Applied Mathematics} \textbf{3}(1), 1--8 (1981).
doi:10.1016/0166-218X(81)90022-6.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: Let V be a finite ground set and (A_i) an indexed finite family of subsets of V. Repeated member sets are allowed and counted separately. Suppose t >= 1 and each point belongs to at most t members of the family. The Beck–Fiala theorem gives a signing chi: V -> {-1,1} such that the absolute value of the sum of chi over each A_i is at most 2t-1. Empty ground sets, empty families and empty member sets are allowed. This is the classical linear bound, not the open O(sqrt(t)) discrepancy conjecture.
formal_statement: theorem P013 {V I : Type*} [Finite V] [Fintype I] (A : I → Finset V) (t : ℕ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) (hdegree : ∀ v, #{i | v ∈ A i} ≤ t) : BeckFiala.HasDiscrepancyAtMost A (2 * (t : ℤ) - 1)

name: No Rainbow Cycle in the Coordinate Edge-Colouring of the Hypercube
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: The n-dimensional hypercube is the graph whose vertices are the binary strings of length n, with an edge between two strings that differ in exactly one coordinate. Colour each edge by the unique coordinate in which its two endpoints differ — the coordinate (or standard proper) edge-colouring, which uses n colours. A cycle in a graph is rainbow if all of its edges receive distinct colours. The theorem states that, for n ≥ 1, no cycle of the n-dimensional hypercube is rainbow under this colouring: every cycle repeats at least one colour (equivalently, every cycle uses some coordinate direction at least twice).
formal_statement: theorem P014 {hn : 0 < n} {u : Q n} {p : (H n).Walk u u} {hp : IsCycle p} : ¬ IsRainbow (H n) (HEdgeColoring hn) p

name: Ordinary Flats of Given Rank in Complex-Representable Matroids
msc: 05B35 Combinatorial aspects of matroids and geometric lattices
informal_statement_summary: A matroid M on a finite ground set is a combinatorial abstraction of linear independence, given by a rank function on subsets of the ground set; the rank of M is the rank of the whole ground set, and a class of matroids is minor-closed if it is closed under deletions and contractions (taking minors). A flat is a closed set; the rank-1 flats are the points and the rank-2 flats are the lines. A line is ordinary (a two-point line) if it contains exactly two points, and more generally a rank-k flat is ordinary if it is the direct sum of a single point with a rank-(k−1) flat — the higher-rank analogue of an ordinary line. A matroid is complex-representable if it arises from a finite family of vectors in a complex vector space (i.e. is representable over ℂ). The theorem states that for every k ≥ 2, every complex-representable matroid of rank at least 4(k − 1) contains an ordinary flat of rank k. This is the ℂ-representable instance of a theorem of Geelen and Kroeker: for any minor-closed class of matroids admitting a two-point line above some fixed rank C, every member of rank at least C(k − 1) has an ordinary rank-k flat; the constant 4 comes from Kelly's theorem, that every complex-representable matroid of rank at least 4 has a two-point line.
formal_statement: theorem P015 {k : ℕ} (hk : 2 ≤ k) {α : Type} (M : Matroid α) [M.Finite] (hM : IsComplexRepresentable M) (hrank : M.eRank ≥ 4 * (k - 1)) : ∃ F : OrdinaryFlat M, M.eRk F.carrier = k

name: Associativity of the Shao Product of Tensors
msc: 15A69 Multilinear algebra, tensor calculus
informal_statement_summary: Fix a field 𝔽 and a dimension n. An order-m tensor over 𝔽 (with each index ranging over [n] = {0, …, n − 1}) is a function assigning a field element to every m-tuple of indices from [n] — equivalently an element of 𝔽^(nᵐ), an m-dimensional array of side n. The Shao product A ⊡ B of an order-m tensor A and an order-k tensor B is the order-((m − 1)(k − 1) + 1) tensor obtained by a contraction summing over m − 1 paired index families; for m = k = 2 it specialises to ordinary matrix multiplication, and when both factors have order at least 3 the order of the product strictly exceeds those of the factors. The theorem states that the Shao product is associative: for tensors A, B, C of orders m, k, l (each ≥ 1), (A ⊡ B) ⊡ C = A ⊡ (B ⊡ C). Both sides are tensors of order (m − 1)(k − 1)(l − 1) + 1, and the equality is stated up to the canonical cast identifying these two (equal) index arities.
formal_statement: theorem P016 {m k l : ℕ} (hm : m ≥ 1) (hk : k ≥ 1) (hl : l ≥ 1) (A : Tensor 𝔽 n m) (B : Tensor 𝔽 n k) (C : Tensor 𝔽 n l) : (A ⊡ B) ⊡ C = cast (by grind) (A ⊡ (B ⊡ C))

name: Tutte's Wheel Theorem (3-connected contraction characterization)
msc: 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: A finite graph G is 3-connected if and only if it can be built up from K₄ by edge-uncontractions: there is a sequence G₀ = K₄, G₁, …, Gₙ = G in which each Gᵢ is the contraction Gᵢ₊₁ / xy of an edge xy whose two endpoints both have degree ≥ 3 in Gᵢ₊₁. Companion problem: P020 states the other classical form of Tutte's 1961 Wheel Theorem (single-step deletion/contraction reduction of non-wheel 3-connected graphs); the two formalizations are deliberately kept as distinct targets.
formal_statement: theorem P017 : IsThreeConnected G ↔ HasTutteSequence G

name: Menger's Theorem (vertex connectivity: max disjoint paths = min separator)
msc: 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: Version 1 (set version): for subsets S, T ⊆ V(G) of a finite graph, the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint S–T paths equals the minimum order of an S–T separation. name: Sidorenko's Conjecture for Half-Graphs (universal)
msc: 05C35 Extremal problems in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: For simple graphs H and G, a graph homomorphism H → G is a vertex map sending every edge of H to an edge of G; writing hom(H, G) for the number of such maps, the homomorphism density of H in G is t_H(G) = hom(H, G) / |V(G)|^|V(H)|. Sidorenko's conjecture states that for every bipartite graph H and every graph G, t_H(G) ≥ t_{K₂}(G)^|E(H)|. The half-graph H_r is the bipartite graph on parts {a₁,…,a_r} and {b₁,…,b_r} with an edge a_i b_j exactly when i ≤ j. This challenge asks, for every r, to prove Sidorenko's inequality for the half-graph H_r against every graph G. This case is known: H_r has a vertex complete to the other side (a₁ is adjacent to every b_j, since 1 ≤ j), and Conlon, Fox and Sudakov (Geom. Funct. Anal. 20 (2010), 1354–1366; arXiv:1004.4236) proved Sidorenko's conjecture for every bipartite graph that has a vertex complete to the other side, so the task here is to formalise this known result in Lean.
formal_statement: theorem P021 : ∀ r : ℕ, ∀ (G : SimpleGraph V), SidorenkoFor (halfGraph r) G

name: Failure of the Ubiquity Conjecture for Locally Finite Graphs
msc: 05C83 Graph minors
informal_statement_summary: A graph H is a minor of a graph G if H can be obtained from a subgraph of G by contracting edges, and several copies of H are vertex-disjoint if their vertex sets are pairwise disjoint. A graph is locally finite if every vertex has finite degree. Call H ubiquitous (for the minor relation) if, whenever a graph G contains at least n vertex-disjoint copies of H as minors for every natural number n, then G must contain infinitely many vertex-disjoint copies of H as minors. Andreae's ubiquity conjecture asserts that every locally finite graph is ubiquitous. The theorem refutes it: there exists a locally finite (indeed countable) graph H, every vertex of which has finite degree, together with a host graph G that contains n vertex-disjoint H-minors for every n yet does not contain infinitely many. A concrete witness is the disjoint union of a barbell (a K₅ and a K₃,₃ joined by an edge) with a ray, embedded in a decorated quarter-grid.

name: Full Cube Adjacency by Convex Bodies (universal)
msc: 52A20 Convex sets in n dimensions; 05C62 Graph representations
informal_statement_summary: A convex body in R^d is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. For convex bodies K_1, ..., K_n in R^d, the zone with label I ⊆ [n] is the set of points on none of the boundaries that lie in exactly the bodies K_j with j in I; two zones are adjacent when their closures meet along a relatively open patch of one boundary, and distinct boundaries may not share such a patch. The bodies realise the cube Q_n when all 2^n zones are nonempty and connected and the labelled region-adjacency graph is exactly Q_n. For arbitrary tame spheres, Q_n is realisable in R^2 exactly for n ≤ 3, in R^3 exactly for n ≤ 4 (an obstruction via the Conway–Gordon theorem), and in R^d for every n when d ≥ 4; for round spheres the threshold is n ≤ d + 1, and convex bodies are known to realise Q_n for n ≤ ⌊3d/2⌋. The theorem states that, for every d ≥ 4, convex bodies, like tame spheres, realise every Q_n. These results come from unpublished notes (2026) and have not yet been independently reviewed.
formal_statement: theorem P026 : ∀ d : ℕ, 4 ≤ d → ∀ n : ℕ, ConvexCubeRealizable d n

name: Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture
msc: 05C20 Directed graphs (digraphs), tournaments
informal_statement_summary: An oriented graph is a loopless directed graph with no 2-cycles (an orientation of a simple graph). For a vertex v, the first out-neighbourhood N+(v) is the set of vertices v points to, and the second out-neighbourhood N++(v) is the set of vertices at directed distance exactly two from v (reachable by a 2-step directed path but not out-neighbours of v). Seymour's Second Neighbourhood Conjecture (c. 1990) states that every finite oriented graph has a vertex v with |N+(v)| <= |N++(v)|. The tournament case is Dean's conjecture, proved by Fisher (1996); the general case was open until October 2026, when a proof appeared in OpenAI's math release (Lean-checked, not yet independently verified). The formal statement requires the vertex set to be nonempty.
formal_statement: theorem P027 {V : Type*} [Finite V] [Nonempty V] (G : OrientedGraph V) : ∃ v, (G.outNeighborhood v).ncard ≤ (G.secondOutNeighborhood v).ncard

name: Tutte-type canonical decomposition of 3- and 4-connected graphs (Main Theorem 1)
msc: 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: Tutte's classical decomposition splits a 2-connected graph canonically into 3-connected pieces, cycles and bonds arranged in a tree structure. Kurkofka and Planken ('A Tutte-type canonical decomposition of 3- and 4-connected graphs') extend this one level up using tetra-separations: pairs (A, B) covering the vertex set whose separator, made of the vertices in A ∩ B and the edges between A \ B and B \ A, has size four, with every separator vertex having two neighbours on each side and the separator edges forming a matching. Main Theorem 1 (with Remark 1.2), stated in the problem file as MainTheorem1Statement, says that for every 4-connected finite graph G the mixed-tree-decomposition determined by the totally-nested tetra-separations (the separations induced by its oriented tree edges are exactly these, bijectively) exists, is invariant under the automorphisms of G, and that each of its torsos is quasi-5-connected, a cycle of triangle-torsos and 3-connected torsos on at most 5 vertices, a generalised double-wheel, or a thickened K_{4,m}, unless G itself is a sprinkled K_{4,m} with m ≥ 4.

name: Reduction lemma for polychromatic colourings via shallow hitting sets (Lemma 3)
msc: 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 29: Polychromatic Colourings of Geometric Hypergraphs via Shallow Hitting Sets}
\refstepcounter{section}

\begin{definition}[Range-capturing hypergraph]
A \emph{range family} in $\R^d$ is a collection $R$ of subsets of $\R^d$ (for instance, all axis-aligned strips, all bottomless rectangles, or all halfplanes). A finite point set $V \subseteq \R^d$ is in \emph{general position} if any two distinct points of $V$ differ in every coordinate. Fix a range family $R$, a finite point set $V$ in general position, and an integer $m \geq 1$. The \emph{$m$-uniform range-capturing hypergraph} $H\ev{V, R, m}$ has vertex set $V$, and a subset $e \subseteq V$ is a hyperedge precisely when $|e| = m$ and $e$ is \emph{captured} by some range $\rho \in R$, that is, $e = V \cap \rho$ (the points of $V$ lying in $\rho$ are exactly those of $e$).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Polychromatic colouring and the parameter $m_R(k)$]
For an integer $k \geq 1$, a colouring $c \colon V \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ is \emph{polychromatic} for a hypergraph on $V$ if every hyperedge $e$ contains at least one vertex of each colour, i.e.\ $\{c(v) : v \in e\} = \{1, \dots, k\}$. The hypergraph is \emph{polychromatically $k$-colourable} if such a colouring exists. Define
$$
m_R(k) := \min\{\, m : H\ev{V, R, m} \text{ is polychromatically } k\text{-colourable for every finite } V \text{ in general position} \,\}.
$$
Clearly $m_R(k) \geq k$, and the ``gold standard'' is a \emph{linear} upper bound $m_R(k) = O(k)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$t$-shallow hitting set]
For an integer $t \geq 1$, a subset $X \subseteq V$ is a \emph{$t$-shallow hitting set} of a hypergraph on $V$ if
$$
1 \ \leq\ |e \cap X| \ \leq\ t \qquad \text{for every hyperedge } e,
$$
i.e.\ $X$ meets every hyperedge at least once but at most $t$ times. We say $R$ \emph{admits uniform $t$-shallow hitting sets at uniformity $m$} if every $H\ev{V, R, m}$ (with $V$ finite and in general position) has a $t$-shallow hitting set.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shrinkable range family]
A range family $R$ is \emph{shrinkable} if for every finite point set $V$ in general position and every $m \geq 1$, each hyperedge of $H\ev{V, R, m}$ contains a hyperedge of $H\ev{V, R, m-1}$.
\end{definition}

The central message of \cite{plankenueckerdt}, building on the abstract shallow-hitting-set framework of Keszegh and P\'alv\"olgyi \cite{keszeghpalvolgyi}, is that constant-size shallow hitting sets ($t = O(1)$ independent of $m$) force a linear polychromatic bound. The following reduction lemma (Lemma 3 of \cite{keszeghpalvolgyi}, in the presentation of \cite{plankenueckerdt}) isolates the purely combinatorial colouring step from the geometric constructions.

\begin{theorem}[Reduction lemma: shallow hitting sets imply a linear polychromatic bound]\label{shallowmain}
Let $R$ be a shrinkable range family in $\R^d$ and let $t, k \geq 1$. If $R$ admits uniform $t$-shallow hitting sets at every uniformity $m \geq 1$, then $m_R(k) \leq t(k-1) + 1$; that is, for every finite point set $V$ in general position the hypergraph $H\ev{V, R, t(k-1)+1}$ admits a polychromatic $k$-colouring.
\end{theorem}

The substance of \cite{plankenueckerdt} is then verifying the shallow-hitting hypothesis with a \emph{constant} $t$ for concrete geometric range families --- all axis-aligned strips in $\R^d$, all bottomless and all topless rectangles in $\R^2$, and all unit-height axis-aligned rectangles in $\R^2$ --- thereby improving previously known polynomial bounds on $m_R(k)$ to $O(k)$. The shallow-hitting route to linear polychromatic colourings goes back to Smorodinsky and Yuditsky \cite{smorodinskyyuditsky}, who established $2$-shallow hitting sets (hence $m_R(k) \leq 2k - 1$) for halfplanes.

\paragraph{Formalisation notes.} Points are elements of $\R^d$, a range family is an arbitrary set of subsets of $\R^d$, and every quantification over point sets $V$ ranges over finite sets in general position. The conclusion is stated as the polychromatic $k$-colourability of every $H\ev{V, R, t(k-1)+1}$; the form $m_R(k) \leq t(k-1)+1$ is recorded as a corollary, with $m_R(k)$ formalised as the infimum of the uniformities $m$ that work (the infimum of the empty set being $0$).

A colouring of V with k colours is polychromatic for H(V,R,m) if every hyperedge contains all k colours, and m_R(k) is the least uniformity m such that every H(V,R,m) admits a polychromatic k-colouring. informal_statement_summary: Stallings' theorem characterizes the infinite finitely generated groups with more than one end as those splitting over a finite subgroup. The paper 'Towards a Stallings-type theorem for finite groups' by Carmesin, Kontogeorgiou, Kurkofka and Turner develops a finite analogue in which ends are replaced by r-local separators of Cayley graphs. The formalized main theorem states, for a finite nilpotent group Γ of nilpotency class at most n and any r ≥ max(4^{n+1}, 20), the equivalence (TFAE) of three assertions: (I) the r-local covering of some Cayley graph of Γ has at least two ends separated by at most two vertices; (II) some Cayley graph of Γ has an r-local cutvertex or an r-local 2-separator, and |Γ| > r; (III) Γ is isomorphic to C_i × C_j with i > r and j ∈ {1, 2}. The r-local covering G_r (the covering whose characteristic subgroup is generated by the closed walks of length at most r) is characterised intrinsically: a covering map (closed-neighbourhood bijections) with connected cover, in which distinct lifts of a vertex are at distance greater than r and every closed walk of the cover is transformed into the trivial walk by inserting and deleting closed subwalks of length at most r.
formal_statement: theorem P037 [Finite Γ] [Group.IsNilpotent Γ] {n r : ℕ} (hclass : Group.nilpotencyClass Γ ≤ n) (hr : max (4 ^ (n + 1)) 20 ≤ r) : [AssertionI Γ r, AssertionII Γ r, AssertionIII Γ r].TFAE

name: Thomassen's Conjecture (4-connected line graphs are Hamiltonian)
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: The line graph L(G) of a finite simple graph G has the edges of G as its vertices, two of them adjacent iff the corresponding edges share an endvertex. A graph is k-connected if it has more than k vertices and stays connected after deleting any fewer than k vertices, and Hamiltonian if it has a cycle through all vertices. Thomassen's conjecture (1986) asserts that every 4-connected line graph is Hamiltonian. By Ryjáček's closure it is equivalent to the Matthews–Sumner conjecture (4-connected claw-free graphs are Hamiltonian); 7-connected line graphs are Hamiltonian (Zhan 1991), as are 5-connected line graphs of minimum degree at least 6 (Kaiser–Vrána 2012). Via Harary–Nash-Williams it is equivalent to: every essentially 4-edge-connected graph has a dominating closed trail; by Fleischner–Jackson the cubic case (cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs have dominating cycles) is already equivalent to the full conjecture.
formal_statement: theorem P038 (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (h4 : (lineGraph G).IsVertexConnected 4) : (lineGraph G).IsHamiltonian

name: A Fully Adaptive Strategy for Hamiltonian Cycles in the Semi-Random Graph Process (Gao–MacRury–Prałat, Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C80 Random graphs; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Gao, MacRury and Pralat (2022): the Hamiltonian-cycle threshold of the semi-random graph process satisfies tau_HAM <= 2.01678: for every q < 1 and epsilon > 0 and all large n, some fully adaptive strategy (one that sees the whole history) builds a Hamiltonian cycle on [n] with probability at least q within (2.01678 + epsilon) n rounds. The constant is the numerical solution of the paper's differential equations for the DegreeGreedy, FullyRandomized and clean-up phases.
formal_statement: theorem P039 : tau hamiltonianProperty ≤ 2.01678

name: A Recolouring Version of a Conjecture of Reed (odd holes and Kempe changes)
msc: 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A Kempe change in a properly k-coloured graph swaps the two colours of a maximal connected bichromatic component (a Kempe chain); a graph is k-recolourable when any two of its k-colourings are joined by a sequence of Kempe changes. With ω(v) the largest clique containing v and deg(v) the degree, the paper's local parameter is f(G) = max_v ⌈(ω(v) + deg(v) + 1)/2⌉, the local analogue of Reed's bound ⌈(ω(G) + Δ(G) + 1)/2⌉. An odd hole is an induced cycle of odd length at least 5, and a k-colouring is frozen when every two colour classes induce a connected subgraph, so no Kempe change alters the colour partition. Theorem 4 of De Meyer et al. (arXiv:2502.10147) has two parts, packaged here as one target: (i) if every odd hole of G contains a vertex of degree at most f(G), then G is k-recolourable for every k > f(G); (ii) for every k ≥ 3 there is a perfect graph with a non-unique frozen k-colouring — hence not k-recolourable — where k is exactly one below the Reed half-bound ⌈(ω(G) + Δ(G) + 1)/2⌉. In particular odd-hole-free graphs realise ε = 1/2 in the paper's recolouring version of Reed's conjecture, tight up to one colour even on perfect graphs.
formal_statement: theorem P040 : ReedRecolouringOddHoles ∧ FrozenPerfectGraphs

name: 3-SAT as an allocation-constraint system
msc: 68R05 Combinatorics in computer science; 03B05 Propositional logic
informal_statement_summary: A 3-CNF formula over n Boolean variables is a finite list of clauses, each an ordered triple of literals (a variable or its negation); it is satisfiable when some truth assignment makes at least one literal of every clause true. On the other side, an allocation assigns a Boolean value to each of 2n houses, where house 2i carries the literal x_i and house 2i+1 carries its negation. The constraint system consists of the NEQ constraints on the complementary pairs (2i, 2i+1) — the two houses of a variable must receive opposite values — and, for each clause, an OR constraint requiring one of the three houses carrying its literals to be true. The problem: a 3-CNF formula is satisfiable if and only if this constraint system has a solution. This is the glossed-over combinatorial step of Lemma 3.2 in Carmesin–Turner, 'Hardness of Planarity for Weak Temporal Sequences of 2-Connected Graphs' (arXiv:2512.06403), where such allocation constraints are realised geometrically by housing sequences. Known-true; both directions require constructing the translation and verifying it, and nothing can be discharged vacuously since the statement has no free hypothesis fields.
formal_statement: theorem P041 (F : ThreeCNF) : F.Satisfiable ↔ ∃ f : Allocation (2 * F.numVars), f ∈ NEQ (complementaryPairs F.numVars) ∩ ORConstraints (clauseTriples F)

name: The Riemann Hypothesis
msc: 11M26 Nonreal zeros of zeta and L-functions
informal_statement_summary: The Riemann zeta function, defined for re(s) > 1 by the Dirichlet series sum n^(-s) and extended to the complex plane by analytic continuation, vanishes at the trivial zeros s = -2, -4, -6, .... The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that every other zero — every nontrivial zero, i.e. every s with zeta(s) = 0 that is not a trivial zero and not the pole location s = 1 — lies on the critical line re(s) = 1/2. The formal statement is Mathlib's own definition RiemannHypothesis. The problem has been open since Riemann's 1859 memoir and is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems.
formal_statement: theorem P042 : RiemannHypothesis

name: Shallow hitting edge sets in uniform hypergraphs (Theorem 2.4)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A finite multihypergraph consists of a finite vertex set, a finite set of edge labels, and a support map assigning each label a set of vertices contained in the vertex set (distinct labels may share a support, modelling parallel edges). It is r-uniform when every edge has exactly r vertices, and μ-near-regular when there are degree witnesses 0 < δ ≤ Δ with Δ ≤ μ·δ such that every vertex has degree between δ and Δ. A set M of edges is a t-shallow hitting edge set if every vertex lies in at least one and at most t edges of M. Theorem 2.4 of the paper 'Shallow Hitting Edge Sets in Uniform Hypergraphs' asserts a single threshold function t(μ, r) with the asymptotics t(μ, r) = e·μ·r·(1 + o_{μr}(1)) — formalized as a limit along the filter where μ·r tends to infinity — such that every r-uniform μ-near-regular finite multihypergraph admits a t(μ, r)-shallow hitting edge set. The paper's proof is probabilistic, via the Lovász Local Lemma and Stirling's formula. Compared to the drafting stage, the existential over t is quantified outside the vertex and label types, so one threshold function must work for all hypergraphs, as in the paper.
formal_statement: theorem P043 : ∃ t : ℝ → ℕ → ℕ, PaperTheorem24Asymptotic t ∧ ∀ (W J : Type u) [DecidableEq W] [DecidableEq J] (μ : ℝ) (r : ℕ) (H : FiniteMultiHypergraph W J), 0 < μ → 1 ≤ r → H.IsUniform r → H.IsNearRegular μ → H.HasShallowHittingEdgeSet (t μ r)

name: Whitney's uniqueness theorem
msc: 05C10 Planar graphs; geometric and topological aspects of graph theory
informal_statement_summary: A rotation system on a finite simple graph is a permutation of its darts (directed edges) acting as a single cycle on the darts at each vertex — combinatorially, a cellular embedding of the graph into oriented surfaces (Heffter–Edmonds). A rotation system is planar when its Euler characteristic #V − #E + #F attains the bound 2 per connected component, i.e. every component is embedded in a sphere; the reflection of a rotation system reverses the cyclic order at every vertex (the mirror embedding). Whitney's uniqueness theorem (1932) states that a 3-connected planar graph has an essentially unique embedding: any two planar rotation systems coincide, or coincide after reflection. 3-connectivity is `SimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 3` from the shared library. This is the classical tool behind, e.g., the temporal-planarity work of Carmesin and Turner; the rotation-system vocabulary lives in the statement library (Mathlib_Problems/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/RotationSystem.lean).
formal_statement: theorem P044 {V : Type u} [Finite V] {G : SimpleGraph V} (h3 : G.IsVertexConnected 3) {R₁ R₂ : G.RotationSystem} (h₁ : R₁.IsPlanar) (h₂ : R₂.IsPlanar) : R₂ = R₁ ∨ R₂ = R₁.reflect

name: Rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings (Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: An edge-colouring of a simple graph is proper when adjacent edges (edges sharing an endpoint, i.e. adjacent vertices of the line graph) receive distinct colours, and a cycle is rainbow when its edges have pairwise distinct colours. The average degree of a finite graph is 2|E|/|V|. Theorem 1.1 of 'Essentially tight bounds for rainbow cycles in proper edge-colourings' asserts an absolute constant C > 0 such that every properly edge-coloured graph on n >= 3 vertices with average degree at least C * log n * log log n contains a rainbow cycle. The formalization states this as the log n * log log n instance of a parameterised threshold statement RainbowCycleThreshold f. The lower-bound constructions discussed in the paper have average degree Omega(log n) and no rainbow cycle, leaving a log log n gap to this upper bound. This problem shares its source paper with P014, which formalizes the paper's hypercube lemma; here the target is the main theorem.
formal_statement: theorem P045 : RainbowCycleThreshold.{u, v} (fun n => Real.log n * Real.log (Real.log n))

name: Clustered Hajós (Liu–Wood, Theorem 6)
msc: 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C83 Graph minors
informal_statement_summary: A vertex coloring (adjacent vertices may share a color) has clustering η when every connected monochromatic component has at most η vertices; a graph is clusteredly k-colorable with clustering η when such a coloring with k colors exists. A graph contains a subdivision of K_n when it has n distinct branch vertices joined, for each pair, by internally disjoint paths (the standard path model, formalized by nonempty simple vertex lists chained along edges). Hajós conjectured that graphs with no K_(s+1)-subdivision are properly s-colorable; Catlin disproved this for s ≥ 6. Theorem 6 of Liu and Wood, 'Clustered Variants of Hajós' Conjecture', rescues the conjecture in the clustered setting: for every s there is an η = η(s) such that every finite graph containing no subdivision of K_(s+1) admits a coloring with max(4s − 5, 1) colors and clustering η. The paper's proof relies on two companion papers and the Liu–Thomas structure theorem for graphs excluding a bounded-degree subdivision.
formal_statement: theorem P046 (s : ℕ) : ∃ η : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V), ¬ IsCliqueSubdivision G (s + 1) → ClusterColorable G (max (4 * s - 5) 1) η

name: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture (Kühn–Sauermann–Steiner–Wigderson, Theorem 1.3)
msc: 05C83 Graph minors; 05C15 Colouring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: An odd K_t minor of G is a system of t vertex-disjoint trees in G, each equipped with a proper 2-coloring, such that every two trees are joined by an edge of G whose endpoints receive matching colors in their respective trees. The odd Hadwiger conjecture (Gerards–Seymour, 1993) asserts that graphs with no odd K_t minor are properly (t−1)-colorable. Theorem 1.3 of Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson, 'Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture', refutes this in a strong multiplicative sense: for every δ > 0 and all sufficiently large t there is a graph with no odd K_t minor whose chromatic number is at least (3/2 − δ)t. The construction takes complements of pseudorandom triangle-free graphs, which have independence number 2 and hence chromatic number at least n/2, and shows via a stability analysis that odd clique minors in such graphs cannot exceed order about n/3.
formal_statement: theorem P047 : ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ t₀ : ℕ, ∀ t : ℕ, t₀ ≤ t → ∃ n : ℕ, ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), HasPaperChromaticLowerBound G δ t ∧ OddCliqueMinorFree G t

name: A hypergraph bandwidth theorem (Lang–Sanhueza-Matamala, Theorem 3.5)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: For a k-uniform hypergraph G, tight connectivity means no isolated vertices plus connectivity of the line graph on E(G) whose adjacency is overlap in exactly k−1 vertices; a component is an edge-maximal spanning tightly connected subhypergraph. A Hamilton framework for a family P of s-vertex t-graphs selects in each member a component with a perfect fractional matching (total weight n/t) and an aperiodic closed tight walk (order 1 mod t), consistently across members obtained by deleting distinct vertices from a common (s+1)-vertex graph (F1-F4 of Definition 3.1). The t-clique graph of G has as edges the t-sets all of whose k-subsets are edges. G s-robustly satisfies P when the s-uniform property graph, whose edges are the s-sets inducing a member of P, has minimum 2t-degree at least (1 − 1/s²)·C(n−2t, s−2t). Theorem 3.5 of Lang and Sanhueza-Matamala, 'A hypergraph bandwidth theorem', asserts: for all k, t, s there are c > 0 and n₀ such that every k-graph G on n ≥ n₀ vertices whose clique graph robustly satisfies a family admitting a Hamilton framework contains every n-vertex blow-up of the (t−k+1)-st power of a tight k-cycle with clusters of size at most (log log n)^c. This unifies and extends the known Dirac-type Hamiltonicity results for hypergraphs to the bandwidth setting.
formal_statement: theorem P048 (k t s : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) (hkt : k ≤ t) (hts : 2 * t ≤ s) : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} {W : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype W], ∀ (P : Set (Hypergraph (Fin s))) (G : Hypergraph V) (H : Hypergraph W), n₀ ≤ Fintype.card V → Fintype.card W = Fintype.card V → IsSpanning G → IsUniform k G → AdmitsHamiltonFramework t s P → RobustlySatisfies t s (cliqueGraph k t G) P → IsBlowUpOfCyclePower H k t c → Embeds H G

name: Counting perfect matchings in Dirac hypergraphs (Kwan–Safavi–Wang, Theorem 1.7)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C30 Enumeration in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: For 1 ≤ d < k, let m_d(k,n) be the minimum d-degree forcing a perfect matching in an n-vertex k-uniform hypergraph (n divisible by k), and let α_d(k) = lim m_d(k,n)/C(n−d,k−d) be the asymptotic Dirac threshold (the limit exists by Ferber–Kwan; its value is a major open problem for most d, k). A fractional perfect matching assigns weights in [0,1] to edges with unit sum at every vertex; its entropy is Σ x_e log(1/x_e), and h(G) is the supremum of these entropies. Theorem 1.7 of Kwan, Safavi and Wang, 'Counting Perfect Matchings in Dirac Hypergraphs', extends the Cuckler–Kahn theorem to hypergraphs: for fixed γ > 0, every family of k-graphs with minimum d-degree at least (α_d(k)+γ)C(n−d,k−d) has Φ(G) = e^{h(G)}(1/e + o(1))^{(1−1/k)n} perfect matchings. The formalization states the equivalent logarithmic form: the normalized error (log Φ(G) − h(G) + (1−1/k)n)/n tends to zero along every such family, indexed by n = km.
formal_statement: theorem P049 (d k : ℕ) (hd : 1 ≤ d) (hdk : d < k) (γ α : ℝ) (hγ : 0 < γ) (hα : IsAsymptoticDiracThreshold d k α) (G : (m : ℕ) → Hypergraph (Fin (k * m))) (hG : IsDiracFamily d k γ α G) : HasEntropyCountingAsymptotic k G

name: Dirac's theorem for linear hypergraphs (Im–Lee, Theorem 1.2)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C07 Vertex degrees
informal_statement_summary: A k-uniform hypergraph is linear when any two distinct edges share at most one vertex. Theorem 1.2 of Im and Lee, 'Dirac's theorem for linear hypergraphs', generalizes Dirac's theorem: for every ε > 0 and k ≥ 2 there are constants C and n₀ such that every n-vertex linear k-graph with n ≥ n₀ and minimum vertex degree at least n/k + C contains a matching covering at least (1−ε)n vertices. The case k = 2 follows from Dirac's theorem; the degree condition is asymptotically best possible by a construction from mutually orthogonal Latin squares (Proposition 1.3). The proof determines the perfect fractional matching threshold for linear hypergraphs via Farkas' lemma, then regularizes and applies the Pippenger–Spencer semirandom method.
formal_statement: theorem P050 (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) : ∃ C n₀ : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ 0 < n₀ ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, n₀ ≤ n → ∀ H : Hypergraph (Fin n), IsSpanning H → IsUniform k H → IsLinear H → (n : ℝ) / (k : ℝ) + (C : ℝ) ≤ (minimumVertexDegree H : ℝ) → HasAlmostPerfectMatching H ε

name: Helly number for agreeing orders of marked cliques (Biró–Lehel–Tóth, Theorem 1)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 06A05 Total orders; 52A35 Helly-type theorems
informal_statement_summary: A 2-extreme marked r-uniform clique on a vertex set V assigns to every r-subset (edge) a distinguished 2-element boundary set contained in it. A linear order (formalized by a rank function injective on the relevant subset) agrees with the marking on U ⊆ V when, for every edge inside U, the two boundary vertices are the minimum and maximum of the edge. Theorem 1 of Biró, Lehel and Tóth, 'Helly-type theorems for the ordering of the vertices of a hypergraph', is a Helly-type theorem: for r ≥ 3, a marked clique on at least 2r−2 vertices admits a globally agreeing linear order if and only if every subset of 2r−2 vertices does. The number 2r−2 is sharp. The case r = 3 is of particular interest in the axiomatic theory of betweenness. [Statement adopted 2026-09-08 from the vb/Folders formalisation: the conclusion now includes the sharpness clause HasSharpExample r, that some 2-extreme marked r-clique on 2r − 2 vertices has agreeing orders on all (2r − 3)-subsets but no global one.]
formal_statement: theorem P051 (r : ℕ) (hr : 3 ≤ r) : (∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V], 2 * r - 2 ≤ Fintype.card V → ∀ H : TwoExtremeMarkedClique V r, H.HasAgreeingOrderOn Finset.univ ↔ H.HasLocalAgreeingOrders (2 * r - 2)) ∧ HasSharpExample r

name: Distinct clique sizes in uniform hypergraphs (Gao, Theorem 1.1; Erdős problem #775)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C69 Vertex subsets with special properties; 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: In a k-uniform hypergraph, a complete set is a vertex set all of whose k-subsets are edges, and a clique is an inclusion-maximal complete set. Theorem 1.1 of Jun Gao, 'On cliques in hypergraphs', shows that for every k ≥ 3 and every constant C there is N(k,C) such that every n-vertex k-uniform hypergraph with n ≥ N has at most n − C distinct clique sizes — equivalently, the maximal possible deficit f(n,k) = n − g(n,k) tends to infinity. The 3-uniform case answers a question of Erdős (problem #775). For graphs (k = 2) the story goes back to Moon–Moser (1965), and Erdős's construction shows f(n,3) ≤ log* n, so the growth of the deficit is genuinely slow. The proof orders maximal cliques by size and builds a (k−1,C)-layered rooted tree whose order is bounded in terms of k and C alone.
formal_statement: theorem P052 (k C : ℕ) (hk : 3 ≤ k) : ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → ∀ H : Hypergraph (Fin n), IsSpanning H → IsUniform k H → distinctCliqueSizeCount k H ≤ n - C

name: Hypergraph joints (Chao–Yu, Theorem 1.12)
msc: 52C35 Arrangements of points, flats, hyperplanes; 05D99 Extremal combinatorics; 51A20 Configuration theorems in linear incidence geometry
informal_statement_summary: Fix a multihypergraph H on [d] with edges colored by [r] so that color i consists of distinct edges of cardinality d − k_i (1 ≤ k_i ≤ d−1). Given, for each color, a finite indexed family of k_i-dimensional affine flats in F^d, a point p is an H-joint if flats can be selected, one per edge, together with an invertible affine map A with A(0) = p, such that each selected flat is the A-image of the coordinate subspace complementary to its edge. Theorem 1.12 of Chao and Yu, 'When Joints Meet Extremal Graph Theory: Hypergraph Joints', bounds the number of H-joints by C_{H,w}·|F₁|^{w̄₁}⋯|F_r|^{w̄_r} for every fractional cover w of H, with the explicit constant C_{H,w} = d!^{|w|−1}·∏_i (1/k_i!)^{w̄_i}·∏_e (w(e)/w̄_{c(e)})^{w(e)}. The classical joints theorem (Guth–Katz type, sharp constant, over every field) is the one-color instance; the theorem also yields the partial shadow phenomenon of Bollobás–Eccles via projected configurations.
formal_statement: theorem P053 {d r : ℕ} (H : ColoredMultiHypergraph d r) (k : Fin r → ℕ) (hk : ∀ i, 1 ≤ k i ∧ k i ≤ d - 1) (hUniform : IsUniformlyColored H k) (w : Fin H.edgeCount → ℝ) (hw : WeightCovers H w) (𝔽 : Type*) [Field 𝔽] (C : HJointConfiguration d r H 𝔽 k) : (C.joints.card : ℝ) ≤ jointConstant H k w * flatFamilyProduct C w

name: Cycle Double Cover Conjecture
msc: 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties; 05C40 Connectivity; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: A finite multigraph may have loops and parallel edges. An edge is a bridge if deleting it separates its two endpoints, and the graph is bridgeless when it has no bridge. A cycle is a nonempty inclusion-minimal edge set having even degree at every vertex; thus a loop is a one-edge cycle and two parallel edges can form a two-edge cycle. A cycle double cover is a finite multiset of cycles, represented by a list so repetitions are retained, in which every edge occurs exactly twice. The cycle double cover conjecture asserts that every finite bridgeless multigraph has a cycle double cover.
formal_statement: theorem P054 {V : Type u} {E : Type v} [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] [Finite V] [Fintype E] (G : Multigraph V E) (hG : G.Bridgeless) : Nonempty G.CycleDoubleCover

name: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: The graph is the same finite multigraph used by the cycle double cover problem. It is assumed simple, its underlying simple graph is regular of degree three, and it is 2-connected in the shared vertex-connectivity sense (SimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 2: more than two vertices, and still connected after deleting any one vertex). A circuit reuses the existing definition of a cycle as a nonempty inclusion-minimal even edge set. A circuit double cover is represented canonically by assigning multiplicity zero, one, or two to every circuit so that every edge has total multiplicity exactly two; this avoids counting orderings of the same family as different covers. Every properly 3-edge-coloured graph satisfying these hypotheses on n vertices has at least 2^(n/2 - 1) circuit double covers.
formal_statement: theorem P055 {V E : Type*} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (G : Multigraph V E) (hSimple : G.IsSimple) (hCubic : G.toSimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree 3) (hG : G.toSimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 2) (c : G.ProperThreeEdgeColoring) : 2 ^ (Fintype.card V / 2 - 1) ≤ G.circuitDoubleCovers.card

name: Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers at High Girth
msc: 05C38 Paths and cycles; 05C40 Connectivity; 05C21 Flows in graphs
informal_statement_summary: The graph is the same finite multigraph used by the cycle double cover problem, with circuit double covers recorded canonically by cycle multiplicities. Here the graph is simple, cubic, and 3-connected in the shared vertex-connectivity sense (SimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 3: more than three vertices, and still connected after deleting any two), and has girth at least 16: every cycle, in the inclusion-minimal even edge set sense, has at least sixteen edges. Theorem 1.8 of Hušek and Šámal, 'Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers', asserts a uniform exponential rate: there is c > 0 and a threshold n₀ such that every such graph on n ≥ n₀ vertices has at least 2^(cn) circuit double covers. Unlike Theorem 1.7 (Problem 55), no 3-edge-colorability is assumed, so the result covers high-girth snarks — historically the presumed hard case of the cycle double cover conjecture. The threshold 16 comes from the margin 16 > 6·log₂6 ≈ 15.51.
formal_statement: theorem P056 : ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ {V : Type u} {E : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (G : Multigraph V E), G.IsSimple → G.toSimpleGraph.IsRegularOfDegree 3 → G.toSimpleGraph.IsVertexConnected 3 → G.HasGirthAtLeast 16 → n₀ ≤ Fintype.card V → (2 : ℝ) ^ (c * Fintype.card V) ≤ G.circuitDoubleCovers.card

name: Divisorial Gonality of Finite Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: A divisor is an integer-valued chip configuration on the vertices of a finite loopless multigraph. Firing a vertex sends one chip along each incident edge, and two divisors are linearly equivalent when their difference is generated by such firings. Every connected multigraph of cycle rank g = |E|-|V|+1 is conjectured to have an effective divisor D of degree at most floor((g+3)/2) whose firing class can place a chip at every prescribed vertex: for each q there is an effective E linearly equivalent to D with E(q) at least one. This is Baker's divisorial gonality conjecture. It is known through genus five and open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P057 (G : CFGraph) (_hConnected : graph_connected G) : ∃ D : CFDiv G, effective D ∧ deg D ≤ (genus G + 3) / 2 ∧ ∀ q : G.V, ∃ E : CFDiv G, effective E ∧ linear_equiv G D E ∧ 1 ≤ E q

name: Brill--Noether Existence for Finite Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: For a connected finite loopless multigraph G, divisors are integer-valued chip configurations modulo chip-firing. A divisor has rank at least r when removing every effective divisor of degree r leaves a firing class containing an effective representative, and it has rank exactly r when this holds for r but not r+1. Given nonnegative integers r and d, let rho(g,r,d) = g - (r+1)(g-d+r), where g = |E(G)|-|V(G)|+1. Baker's Brill--Noether existence conjecture asserts that rho at least zero guarantees a divisor of rank exactly r and degree at most d on every such graph. The conjecture is known for genus at most five and open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P058 (G : CFGraph) (_hConnected : graph_connected G) (r d : ℤ) (_hr : 0 ≤ r) (_hd : 0 ≤ d) (_hρ : 0 ≤ brillNoetherNumber (genus G) r d) : ∃ D : CFDiv G, divisorRankEq G D r ∧ deg D ≤ d

name: Combinatorial Brill--Noether Existence for Metric Graphs
msc: 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra; 14T20 Tropical geometry
informal_statement_summary: A metric graph is represented by a connected finite loopless multigraph whose edge occurrences have positive real lengths. Its points include both vertices and all interior points of the edge intervals. Divisors are finitely supported integer-valued functions on these points, and linear equivalence is generated by divisors of continuous piecewise-affine functions with integral slopes. Given nonnegative integers r and d, let rho(g,r,d) = g - (r+1)(g-d+r). Baker's metric-graph Brill--Noether theorem says that rho at least zero guarantees a divisor of rank exactly r and degree at most d on every metric graph of genus g. Baker's proof passes through classical algebraic Brill--Noether theory, the specialization lemma, and a semicontinuity argument. The challenge is to find a purely combinatorial proof of the same theorem.
formal_statement: theorem P059 (G : MetricGraph) (_hConnected : G.Connected) (r d : ℤ) (_hr : 0 ≤ r) (_hd : 0 ≤ d) (_hρ : 0 ≤ brillNoetherNumber G.genus r d) : ∃ D : MetricDiv G, metricDivisorRankEq G D r ∧ metricDegree D ≤ d

name: Chvátal's Toughness Conjecture
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: The toughness of a finite graph measures how sturdily it is connected: G is t-tough when every vertex set whose deletion disconnects the graph contains at least t vertices per component created (formalized with real t via the component count of the induced graph on the complement). Chvátal's conjecture (1973) asserts that some fixed toughness forces Hamiltonicity: there is t > 0 such that every t-tough graph on at least three vertices has a Hamiltonian cycle. Chvátal's original candidate t = 2 was refuted by Bauer, Broersma and Veldman (2000), who constructed (9/4 − ε)-tough non-Hamiltonian graphs, so any witness satisfies t ≥ 9/4; the conjecture remains open, with t = 3 a natural candidate.
formal_statement: theorem P060 : ∃ t : ℝ, 0 < t ∧ ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V), 3 ≤ Fintype.card V → G.IsTough t → G.IsHamiltonian

name: Seymour's Exact Edge-Colouring Conjecture for Planar Multigraphs
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C10 Planar graphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties
informal_statement_summary: For a loopless multigraph, the degree of a vertex is its number of incident edges, an edge crosses a vertex set when it has one endpoint on each side, and the graph is oddly d-edge-connected when every proper vertex set of odd size is crossed by at least d edges. Planarity is read through the underlying simple graph (parallel edges and loops never obstruct an embedding) using the rotation-system genus-zero characterization of the shared library. Seymour's exact conjecture (1970s) asserts that every d-regular oddly d-edge-connected planar loopless multigraph is d-edge-colourable: its edges can be coloured with d colours so that edges sharing a vertex differ. The case d = 3 is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem (Tait); d = 4, 5 are due to Guenin, d = 6 to Dvořák–Kawarabayashi–Král', and d = 7, 8 to Chudnovsky–Edwards–Kawarabayashi–Seymour. The conjecture is open for every d ≥ 9; without planarity the Petersen graph refutes the statement already at d = 3.
formal_statement: theorem P061 : ∀ (d : ℕ) (V : Type u) (E : Type v) [Fintype V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (M : Multigraph V E), (∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) → M.IsRegular d → M.OddlyEdgeConnected d → M.IsPlanar → M.EdgeColorable d

name: Tutte's 5-Flow Conjecture
msc: 05C21 Flows in graphs; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 62: Tutte's 5-Flow Conjecture}
\refstepcounter{section}

\begin{definition}[Nowhere-zero flows and bridges]
Let $G$ be a multigraph with finitely many edges; loops and parallel edges are allowed. Orient every edge $e$ from a tail $t\ev{e}$ to a head $h\ev{e}$, and let $A$ be an abelian group. A \emph{nowhere-zero $A$-flow} is a map $f \colon E\ev{G} \to A \setminus \{0\}$ satisfying Kirchhoff's law
$$
\sum_{e \,:\, t\ev{e} = v} f\ev{e} \ = \ \sum_{e \,:\, h\ev{e} = v} f\ev{e} \qquad \text{for every vertex } v.
$$
Reversing an edge and negating its value preserves this, so whether $G$ has a nowhere-zero $A$-flow does not depend on the orientation. An edge is a \emph{bridge} if deleting it leaves its two ends in different connected components, and $G$ is \emph{bridgeless} if it has no bridge.
\end{definition}

\begin{openproblem}[Tutte's $5$-flow conjecture]
Prove or disprove: every bridgeless multigraph has a nowhere-zero $\Z/5\Z$-flow.
\end{openproblem}

The conjecture is due to Tutte \cite{tutte1954flows}. By a theorem of Tutte, a graph has a nowhere-zero $A$-flow for one abelian group $A$ of order $k$ exactly when it has one for every such group, and exactly when it has an integer flow with all values in $\{\pm 1, \dots, \pm(k-1)\}$; so the statement above is equivalent to the classical integer form. Jaeger proved that every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero $8$-flow \cite{jaeger1976flows}, and Seymour that it has a nowhere-zero $6$-flow \cite{seymour1981sixflow}. The value $5$ would be best possible, since the Petersen graph has no nowhere-zero $4$-flow. The conjecture holds for planar graphs, where it is dual to the Five Colour Theorem, and for graphs with a Hamiltonian cycle, which even have nowhere-zero $4$-flows. By results of Kochol, a smallest counterexample would be a snark (a bridgeless cubic graph that is not $3$-edge-colourable) that is cyclically $6$-edge-connected \cite{kochol2004reduction} and has girth at least $11$ \cite{kochol2010girth}.

\paragraph{Formalisation notes.} Each edge is oriented by a fixed but arbitrary choice of an ordered pair representing its unordered pair of ends; by the remark above this choice is immaterial. A loop contributes its value to both sides of Kirchhoff's law at its vertex, so it may carry any nonzero value. The edge set is finite, but the vertex set may be infinite; vertices that meet no edge impose no condition. Bridges are as defined above, so a loop is never a bridge, and neither is an edge with a parallel copy.

informal_statement_summary: A nowhere-zero flow on a multigraph assigns a nonzero group value to every edge, in a fixed representative orientation of each edge, so that Kirchhoff's law holds at every vertex; reorienting an edge negates its value, so the orientation choice is immaterial, and loops enter both sides of the law and are unconstrained. Tutte's 5-flow conjecture (1954) asserts that every bridgeless multigraph has a nowhere-zero flow with values in ZMod 5 (by Tutte's theorem only the order of the group matters, so this is equivalent to the classical integer formulation with values of absolute value below five). Jaeger proved the 8-flow theorem and Seymour the 6-flow theorem; five would be best possible, since the Petersen graph has no nowhere-zero 4-flow. For planar graphs the conjecture is the dual of the Five Colour Theorem. A minimal counterexample is, by Kochol's reductions, a cyclically 6-edge-connected snark of girth at least eleven.
