name: Mader's Connectivity Conjecture
msc: 05C40 Connectivity; 05C35 Extremal problems in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: The average degree of a finite simple graph is the sum of its vertex degrees divided by the number of vertices (equivalently twice the edge count over the vertex count). Mader conjectured in 1979 that every graph of average degree at least 3k-1 contains a (k+1)-connected subgraph; the subgraph may be taken induced, since adding edges preserves vertex connectivity. The conjecture has been open for almost half a century: Mader proved in 1972 that average degree 4k-2 suffices, the known sufficient linear factor was improved over the years but never reached 3, and Krone proved the minimum-degree analogue (minimum degree 3k-1 forces a (k+1)-connected subgraph on more than 2k vertices). If true, the bound 3k-1 is sharp for every value of the core connectivity.
formal_statement: theorem P063 : ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (k : ℕ), 1 ≤ k → (3 * k - 1 : ℚ) ≤ G.averageDegree → ∃ s : Set V, (G.induce s).IsVertexConnected (k + 1)

name: The Berge–Fulkerson Conjecture
msc: 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties (factorization, matching); 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A perfect matching of a multigraph is an edge set meeting every vertex in exactly one edge. The Berge-Fulkerson conjecture (Fulkerson 1971) asserts that every bridgeless cubic multigraph has six perfect matchings that together cover every edge exactly twice - equivalently, doubling every edge yields a 6-edge-colourable multigraph. For 3-edge-colourable cubic graphs the six matchings are the three colour classes taken twice, so any counterexample is a snark; the Petersen graph and all verified snark families satisfy the conjecture. By Mazzuoccolo's theorem it is equivalent to Berge's conjecture that five perfect matchings suffice to cover every edge at least once, and it implies the Fan-Raspaud conjecture that three perfect matchings can avoid a common edge.
formal_statement: theorem P064 : ∀ (V : Type u) (E : Type v) [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq E] (M : Multigraph V E), (∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) → M.IsRegular 3 → M.Bridgeless → ∃ P : Fin 6 → Finset E, (∀ i, M.IsPerfectMatchingSet (P i)) ∧ ∀ e : E, (Finset.univ.filter fun i => e ∈ P i).card = 2

name: The Kahn--Kalai Counterexample to Borsuk's Conjecture
msc: 52A20 Convex sets in n dimensions; 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: Borsuk conjectured that every bounded set in d-dimensional Euclidean space can be covered by d+1 subsets of strictly smaller diameter. Kahn and Kalai disproved this in 1993 using the Frankl--Wilson intersection theorem. Their construction on balanced bipartitions of a 52-element set gives a finite set in an affine space of dimension 1325 such that every colouring with 1326 colours has a monochromatic pair at the full diameter. Thus the colour classes cannot all have smaller diameter. The formal statement uses this concrete finite counterexample; finiteness also makes the set automatically bounded. The corrected count has half of C(52,26) points, while a diameter-avoiding subfamily has at most C(51,12) points, so in fact the construction needs at least 1562 smaller-diameter parts.
formal_statement: theorem P065 : ∃ S : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325)), 0 < Metric.diam (S : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325))) ∧ ∀ c : S → Fin 1326, ∃ x y : S, c x = c y ∧ dist x y = Metric.diam (S : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 1325)))

name: The Tangle-Decider Conjecture
msc: 05C40 Connectivity; 05C83 Graph minors; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: An oriented separation of a finite simple graph is a pair (A,B) of vertex sets covering the graph, with no edge between A\B and B\A; its order is |A intersect B|. A k-tangle in Diestel's sense chooses exactly one orientation of every separation of order below k, and no three (not necessarily distinct) chosen small sides induce subgraphs whose union is the whole graph. The tangle-decider conjecture asks whether every such tangle is induced by majority vote by a vertex set X: for every chosen (A,B), |X intersect A| < |X intersect B|. The conjecture is known for k at most 3 and remains open for k at least 4. Every tangle does have an integral weighted decider, and a 2024 finite-reduction theorem reduces each fixed order to connected graphs of size bounded solely in k.
formal_statement: theorem P066 : ∀ (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (τ : G.Tangle k), ∃ X : Finset V, τ.IsDecidedBy X

name: Carmesin–Lichev: Embedding Homologically Trivial Two-Complexes in Exponential Time
msc: 57Q35 Embeddings and immersions; 57M15 Relations with graph theory; 68Q25 Analysis of algorithms and problem complexity; 55N35 Homology and cohomology theories
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 67: Carmesin--Lichev: Embedding Homologically Trivial 2-Complexes in Exponential Time}
\refstepcounter{section}

Embeddability of finite $2$-dimensional simplicial complexes in $\R^3$ is decidable \cite{MatousekEtAl2014Embeddability} but NP-hard \cite{DeMesmayEtAl2017NPHard}. On the promise class of complexes whose integral first homology vanishes, the problem reduces to recognizing the $3$-sphere, and so lies in NP. The challenge asks for a deterministic decision procedure on this class running in time $2^{n^c}$ for some constant $c$.

\begin{definition}[Finite $2$-complex]
A \emph{finite $2$-complex} $K$ is presented by a number $n$ of vertices, labelled $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, together with a list of \emph{edges}, each a pair $\{i, j\}$ written with $i < j$, and a list of \emph{triangles}, each a triple $\{a, b, c\}$ written with $a < b < c$. The presentation is \emph{valid} if the lists have no repetitions, all labels are smaller than $n$, and the three edges $\{a,b\}, \{a,c\}, \{b,c\}$ of every triangle occur in the edge list. Thus a valid presentation is an abstract simplicial complex of dimension at most two on the vertex set $[n]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Boundary maps and trivial first homology]
Orient every edge $\{i, j\}$ ($i < j$) from $i$ to $j$ and every triangle $\{a, b, c\}$ ($a < b < c$) as the cycle $a \to b \to c$. The integral boundary of the edge $e = \{i, j\}$ is $\partial e = j - i$, and the boundary of the triangle $t = \{a, b, c\}$ is
$$
\partial t = \{a, b\} - \{a, c\} + \{b, c\}.
$$
An \emph{integral $1$-chain} is a function $z$ from the edges of $K$ to $\Z$, and it is a \emph{$1$-cycle} if $\sum_e z(e)\,\partial e = 0$, that is, if at every vertex the signed contributions of the incident edges cancel. The complex $K$ has \emph{trivial integral first homology}, $H_1(K; \Z) = 0$, if every integral $1$-cycle is the boundary of an integral $2$-chain: for every $1$-cycle $z$ there is a function $b$ from the triangles of $K$ to $\Z$ with $z = \sum_t b(t)\,\partial t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Geometric realization and embeddability]
The \emph{geometric realization} $|K|$ of $K$ is the subspace of $\R^n$ consisting of the points $x$ with non-negative coordinates summing to $1$ whose support (the set of coordinates $i$ with $x_i \ne 0$) is contained in a vertex, an edge, or a triangle of $K$; it is the union of the standard simplices spanned by the simplices of $K$, with the subspace topology. We say that $K$ \emph{embeds in $\R^3$} if there is a topological embedding $|K| \to \R^3$, that is, a continuous injective map that is a homeomorphism onto its image.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Encoding and running time]
A finite $2$-complex is encoded as the list of natural numbers
$$
n,\ m,\ i_1, j_1, \dots, i_m, j_m,\ k,\ a_1, b_1, c_1, \dots, a_k, b_k, c_k
$$
($m$ edges, $k$ triangles), each number written in binary and the numbers separated by a blank symbol, so that the encoding is a word over a three-letter alphabet from which the complex can be decoded. The running time of a deterministic Turing machine on this encoding is measured in the standard model of Turing machines with finitely many stacks, and the \emph{size} $n$ of an input is the length of its encoding.

For a function $\beta \colon \N \to \N$, say that \emph{embeddability is decidable in time $\beta$} if there are a Boolean function $\mathrm{answer}$ on presentations and a deterministic Turing machine computing $\mathrm{answer}$ from the encoding, such that
\begin{itemize}
\item for every valid presentation $K$ with $H_1(K; \Z) = 0$, $\mathrm{answer}(K)$ is true if and only if $K$ embeds in $\R^3$ (on inputs outside the promise class the answer is unconstrained), and
\item there are constants $C > 0$ and $N$ such that the machine halts within $C\,\beta(n)$ steps on every input of size $n \ge N$.
\end{itemize}
Embeddability is decidable in \emph{polynomial time} if it is decidable in time $n \mapsto n^d$ for some $d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Carmesin--Lichev; Ivanov, Schleimer]\label{thm:embedding}
There is a constant $c$ such that embeddability in $\R^3$ of finite $2$-complexes with trivial integral first homology is decidable in time $n \mapsto 2^{n^c}$.
\end{theorem}

Carmesin and Lichev \cite{CarmesinLichev2022Constructions} observe that, by Carmesin's characterizations \cite{Carmesin2019RotationSystems, Carmesin2019RefinedKuratowski}, deciding embeddability in $3$-space of $2$-complexes with trivial rational first homology is polynomially equivalent to recognizing the $3$-sphere. Sphere recognition lies in NP \cite{Ivanov2008Complexity, Schleimer2011SphereNP}, hence so does the embedding problem on this class, which contains the complexes with trivial integral first homology; an NP procedure runs deterministically in time $2^{n^c}$. Whether polynomial time suffices is open; on complexes with trivial rational first homology it is equivalent to the polynomial sphere recognition problem.

\begin{remark}[Scaling]
The time bound $\beta$ is a parameter of the definition, so the problem scales: one may ask, for each of finitely many values of $a$, whether embeddability is decidable in time $a^n$, in a quasi-exponential bound, or in time $n^a$, obtaining a ladder of statements ordered by the growth of $\beta$. A procedure in time $\beta$ is trivially one in time $\beta'$ whenever $\beta \le C\beta'$ eventually, so each rung implies the rungs with faster-growing bounds.
\end{remark}

informal_statement_summary: A finite two-dimensional simplicial complex is given by numbered vertices together with its edges and triangles. Its integral first homology is trivial when every integral 1-cycle is the boundary of an integral 2-chain. The problem asks for a deterministic algorithm that decides in time 2^(n^c), for some constant c, which such complexes embed topologically in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Embeddability of arbitrary finite 2-complexes in R^3 is decidable and NP-hard. Carmesin and Lichev observe that, by Carmesin's characterizations, embeddability of 2-complexes with trivial rational first homology is polynomially equivalent to 3-sphere recognition, which lies in NP by Ivanov and Schleimer; this gives the exponential bound, while polynomial time remains open. The formalization uses a canonical barycentric realization, explicit integral boundary matrices, a fixed binary encoding, and Mathlib's deterministic Turing-machine runtime model.
formal_statement: theorem P067 : ∃ c, EmbeddabilityInTime fun n ↦ 2 ^ n ^ c

name: Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture
msc: 05C10 Planar graphs; geometric and topological aspects; 05C83 Graph minors; 57M15 Relations with graph theory
informal_statement_summary: A finite planar cover of a graph is a finite planar graph equipped with a surjective graph homomorphism that maps the neighborhood of every covering vertex bijectively onto the neighborhood of its image. Negami's planar-cover conjecture says that a connected graph has such a cover exactly when it embeds in the projective plane. Work on the excluded minors for the projective plane reduces the entire open direction to one graph: the complete multipartite graph K_{1,2,2,2}, equivalently an octahedral graph joined to one apex. The problem asserts that this graph has no finite planar cover. Recent work rules out every cover with fewer than fourteen sheets and imposes strong connectivity constraints on any minimal counterexample, but the unrestricted statement remains open. The formalization defines graph covers directly and expresses planarity through finite planar rotation systems.
formal_statement: theorem P068 : ¬ K1222.HasFinitePlanarCover

name: Algebraic Connectivity of Token Graphs
msc: 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 60J27 Continuous-time Markov processes on discrete state spaces
informal_statement_summary: For a finite graph G on n vertices, the k-token graph has the k-element subsets of the vertex set as its vertices; two configurations are adjacent when one token moves along an edge of G to an unoccupied vertex. Algebraic connectivity is the second-smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian, counted with multiplicity. The theorem states that for every 1 ≤ k < n, the algebraic connectivity of the k-token graph equals that of G. This was originally conjectured in the token-graph literature but is already a consequence of Caputo, Liggett and Richthammer's proof of Aldous' spectral-gap conjecture; the open question is to find a purely combinatorial or algebraic proof. The Lean statement works for disconnected graphs as well and uses Mathlib's ordered Hermitian eigenvalues, so zero eigenvalue multiplicities are represented faithfully.
formal_statement: theorem P069 (V : Type u) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {k : ℕ} (hk₀ : 1 ≤ k) (hkV : k < Fintype.card V) : algebraicConnectivity (tokenGraph G k) = algebraicConnectivity G

name: Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis
msc: 03E35 Consistency and independence results; 03E50 Continuum hypothesis and Martin's axiom
informal_statement_summary: First-order ZFC is deep-embedded in Lean: the language has a single binary membership relation, the eight core axioms and the separation and replacement schemas are spelled out as de Bruijn sentences, and CH is the sentence that every subset of P(omega) injects into omega or receives an injection from P(omega). The problem is three-optioned - prove CH from ZFC, refute it, or prove independence - and exactly one option is provable: the futility certificate. It is unconditional, since Lean's universes provide models of the embedded ZFC; a kernel-checked proof of either other option would witness an inconsistency of Lean itself. Goedel (1938) and Cohen (1963) supply the two model constructions, and the Flypitch project (Han-van Doorn, CPP 2020) formalized exactly this independence in Lean 3, so the problem is solved-in-principle at research level. Consequence is semantic (Mathlib has no syntactic calculus), which agrees with provability by Goedel completeness.
formal_statement: theorem P070 : Independent ZFC CH

name: Bipartite Unique-Neighbour Expanders via Ramanujan Graphs
difficulty: Research (existence form of Asherov–Dinur Theorem 1; the polynomial-time clause is not asserted)
msc: 05C48 Expander graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A bipartite graph is presented by the neighbourhood function of its left side. A right vertex is a unique neighbour of a set S of left vertices if it is adjacent to exactly one member of S, and a (c,d)-biregular unique-neighbour expander family is a uniform threshold delta > 0 together with (c,d)-biregular graphs of arbitrarily large order in which every nonempty set of at most delta|L| left vertices has a unique neighbour. Asherov and Dinur (2023) prove that there is a threshold function q-hat such that for every integer c0 > 5, real alpha > 1 and prime power q > q-hat(c0, alpha) with alpha c0 (q+1) an integer, there is a (c0(q+1), alpha c0 (q+1))-biregular unique-neighbour expander family - arbitrarily unbalanced sides - constructed in polynomial time by composing (q+1, q^3+1)-biregular Ramanujan graphs with a fixed-size gadget through a routed product. The formal statement records the mathematical existence with the paper's degree parameters; explicitness is not captured. Known true at research level: the paper's route needs a new average-degree bound for bipartite Ramanujan graphs, and the non-constructive route needs random biregular graph expansion. (Formalisation upgraded 2026-09-07: the challenge file now defines bipartite multigraphs, the routed product and Lemma 12 itself; the previous thin statement is kept in the attic.)
formal_statement: theorem P071 : ∃ qhat : ℕ → ℝ → ℕ, ∀ c₀ : ℕ, 5 < c₀ → ∀ α : ℝ, 1 < α → ∀ q : ℕ, IsPrimePow q → qhat c₀ α < q → ∀ d : ℕ, (d : ℝ) = α * ((c₀ : ℝ) * ((q : ℝ) + 1)) → ∃ G : ℕ → BipartiteMultigraph, IsUniqueNeighbourExpanderFamily G (c₀ * (q + 1)) d

name: The Anonymous Lower Bound for Superpermutations
msc: 05A05 Permutations, words, matrices; 68R15 Combinatorics on words
informal_statement_summary: A superpermutation on n symbols is a word over an n-letter alphabet containing every permutation of the alphabet as a contiguous factor. In 2011 an anonymous poster on 4chan proved that every superpermutation on n symbols has length at least n! + (n-1)! + (n-2)! + n - 3, improving the Ashlock-Tillotson bound n! + (n-1)! + n - 2; the proof was written up by Houston, Pantone and Vatter in 2018. The bound is tight for n <= 4 (minimal lengths 1, 3, 9, 33) and off by one for n = 5 (minimum 153). The proof counts wasted letters: a letter is wasted unless it completes the first occurrence of a permutation; the first n-1 letters are wasted, each of the (n-1)! cyclic classes of permutations forces a wasted letter upon completion, and each of the (n-2)! trajectories - chains of n-1 cyclic classes linked by single wasted letters - forces a further, distinct wasted letter to change trajectory. The formal statement needs no hypothesis on n, natural-number arithmetic making the small cases trivial. Known true; the combinatorial proof has not been formalized.
formal_statement: theorem P072 : ∀ (n : ℕ) (w : List (Fin n)), IsSuperpermutation n w → n ! + (n - 1)! + (n - 2)! + n - 3 ≤ w.length

name: The Alon–Tarsi Conjecture
msc: 05B15 Orthogonal arrays, Latin squares, Room squares; 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: A Latin square of order n is an n-by-n array of n symbols with no repeated symbol in any row or column; its sign is the product of the signs of its n row permutations and n column permutations, and it is even or odd accordingly. The Alon-Tarsi conjecture (1992) asserts that for every even n the numbers of even and odd Latin squares of order n differ. For odd n >= 3 the two numbers are equal, since swapping two rows is a sign-reversing involution. The conjecture is known for n = p+1 (Drisko 1997) and n = p-1 (Glynn 2010) with p an odd prime, hence for every even n <= 24; the smallest open case is n = 26. By Huang and Rota it implies Rota's basis conjecture in even dimension over characteristic zero, and via the Alon-Tarsi polynomial method it implies the Dinitz conjecture for even n. The signed count is usually computed over row-reduced squares (first row in natural order), which for even n differs from the full signed count by the factor n!.
formal_statement: theorem P073 : ∀ n : ℕ, Even n → (Finset.univ.filter fun L : LatinSquare n => L.sign = 1).card ≠ (Finset.univ.filter fun L : LatinSquare n => L.sign = -1).card

name: The Collatz Conjecture
msc: 11B37 Recurrences; 37P99 Arithmetic and non-Archimedean dynamical systems
informal_statement_summary: The Collatz map sends an even number n to n/2 and an odd n to 3n+1. The Collatz conjecture (1937) asserts that iterating this map from any positive integer eventually reaches 1. It has been verified for all n < 2^68 (Barina 2020); Tao (2019) proved that almost all orbits attain almost bounded values; and any nontrivial cycle would have length at least 17,087,915 (Eliahou 1993, since improved). The conjecture is equivalent to the conjunction of two statements: no orbit diverges, and the only cycle is 1 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1.
formal_statement: theorem P074 : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → CollatzReachesOne n

name: Bounded Avoidability Index of Patterns
msc: 68R15 Combinatorics on words; 05D10 Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: A pattern is a word over variables; it occurs in a word when a non-erasing substitution of the variables by nonempty words turns it into a factor. A pattern is k-avoidable if some infinite word over k letters contains no occurrence of it, and avoidable if it is k-avoidable for some k (Zimin's theorem characterises the avoidable patterns). Currie asked at WORDS 2003 whether there is a pattern that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable, equivalently whether every avoidable pattern is 5-avoidable. Every avoidable binary pattern is 3-avoidable (Cassaigne, Roth), every doubled pattern is 3-avoidable (Ochem 2016), and Clark exhibited a pattern of avoidability index exactly 5, so 5 cannot be lowered; whether the index is bounded at all is open. The challenge asserts the affirmative answer.
formal_statement: theorem P075 : ∀ (m : ℕ) (p : List (Fin m)), IsAvoidable p → IsKAvoidable p 5

name: Conway's 99-Graph Problem
msc: 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A strongly regular graph with parameters (v, k, lambda, mu) is a k-regular graph on v vertices in which adjacent vertices have exactly lambda common neighbours and non-adjacent vertices exactly mu. Conway's 99-graph problem asks whether a strongly regular graph with parameters (99, 14, 1, 2) exists; Conway offered $1000 for a resolution. The parameters pass every known feasibility condition (eigenvalues 3 and -4 with multiplicities 54 and 44, the Krein and absolute bounds); each vertex neighbourhood would be a perfect matching on 14 vertices, so every edge lies in a unique triangle; the sibling parameter sets (9, 4, 1, 2) and (243, 22, 1, 2) are realised by the Paley graph on nine vertices and the Berlekamp-van Lint-Seidel graph. Strong restrictions on the automorphism group of a hypothetical graph are known (Makhnev-Minakova). The problem is open in both directions; a positive answer is equivalent to a symmetric 0/1 matrix A of order 99 with zero diagonal and A^2 = 14I + A + 2(J - I - A), which a computer search could certify.
formal_statement: theorem P076 : ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 99)) (_ : DecidableRel G.Adj), G.IsSRGWith 99 14 1 2

name: The 57-regular Moore Graph
msc: 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs; 05C12 Distance in graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: A Moore graph of degree k and diameter 2 is a k-regular graph of diameter 2 and girth 5; it has k^2 + 1 vertices and is strongly regular with parameters (k^2 + 1, k, 0, 1). Hoffman and Singleton proved that such graphs exist only for k in {2, 3, 7, 57}, and the first three cases are realised by the pentagon, the Petersen graph and the Hoffman-Singleton graph. The problem asks whether the last case exists: is there a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1), i.e. a 57-regular graph of diameter 2 and girth 5 on 3250 vertices? It is open.
formal_statement: theorem P077 : ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)) (_ : DecidableRel G.Adj), G.IsSRGWith 3250 57 0 1

name: The Borodin–Kostochka Conjecture
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C07 Vertex degrees
informal_statement_summary: For a finite simple graph G let chi(G) be the chromatic number, Delta(G) the maximum degree and omega(G) the clique number. Brooks' theorem gives chi(G) <= max(Delta(G), omega(G)) for Delta(G) >= 3. The Borodin-Kostochka conjecture (1977) states that every finite simple graph with maximum degree at least 9 satisfies chi(G) <= max(Delta(G) - 1, omega(G)); equivalently, every graph with Delta >= 9 and omega < Delta is (Delta - 1)-colourable. The threshold 9 is sharp (Catlin graphs). Reed proved the conjecture for Delta >= 10^14, and it is open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P078 : ∀ {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj], 9 ≤ G.maxDegree → G.chromaticNumber ≤ max (G.maxDegree - 1) G.cliqueNum

name: Antipodal Edge-Colourings of the Hypercube
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C38 Paths and cycles
informal_statement_summary: Let d >= 2 and two-colour the edges of the d-dimensional hypercube Q_d so that antipodal edges (an edge and its image under complementing every coordinate) receive opposite colours; no properness is imposed. Norine's conjecture states that some pair of antipodal vertices is then joined by a monochromatic path. The stronger conjecture that every two-colouring of Q_d admits an antipodal path with at most one colour change implies it. A proof for all d ≥ 2 was claimed in July 2026 (Wu–Yang, arXiv:2607.19276); it has not yet been independently verified.
formal_statement: theorem P079 : ∀ (d : ℕ), 2 ≤ d → ∀ c : Sym2 (Q d) → Bool, IsAntipodalColoring d c → ∃ (x : Q d) (w : (H d).Walk x (antipode x)) (b : Bool), IsMonochromatic c w b

name: The Reconstruction Conjecture
msc: 05C60 Isomorphism problems (reconstruction conjecture, etc.)
informal_statement_summary: The card of a finite simple graph G at a vertex v is the vertex-deleted subgraph G - v. Two graphs have the same deck when a bijection sigma between their vertex sets pairs every card G - v with an isomorphic card G' - sigma(v), multiplicities retained and the card isomorphisms independent of each other. The Kelly-Ulam reconstruction conjecture states that two finite simple graphs on at least three vertices with the same deck are isomorphic. Known for disconnected graphs, trees, regular graphs and many other classes, and reducible to 2-connected graphs (Yang); open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P080 : ∀ {V : Type u} {V' : Type v} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (G' : SimpleGraph V'), 3 ≤ Fintype.card V → G.SameDeck G' → Nonempty (G ≃g G')

name: Lovász's Hamiltonian-Path Question for Vertex-Transitive Graphs
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs; 05C25 Graphs and abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields, etc.)
informal_statement_summary: A finite simple graph is vertex-transitive if its automorphism group acts transitively on the vertices. Lovász asked (1969) whether every finite connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path, a path visiting every vertex exactly once. The Hamiltonian-cycle version fails for exactly five known graphs (K_2, Petersen, Coxeter and their truncations), all of which have Hamiltonian paths. Open in general.
formal_statement: theorem P081 : ∀ {V : Type u} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), G.Connected → VertexTransitive G → ∃ (u v : V) (p : G.Walk u v), p.IsPath ∧ p.length + 1 = Fintype.card V

name: Graham's Graph-Pebbling Product Conjecture
msc: 05C76 Graph operations; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: A pebbling configuration assigns a nonnegative integer to each vertex of a graph. A legal move removes two pebbles from one vertex and adds one to an adjacent vertex. The pebbling number π(G) is the least n such that every configuration of n pebbles can place a pebble at any prescribed root using finitely many legal moves. Graham's conjecture asserts π(G □ H) ≤ π(G)π(H) for all finite connected simple graphs G and H, where □ is the Cartesian product. The threshold exists, and requiring exactly n or at least n pebbles gives the same number. The conjecture is open; the companion DISPROVE file asks for finite connected factors violating the inequality.
formal_statement: theorem P082 : ∀ {V : Type u} {W : Type v} [Fintype V] [Fintype W] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq W] (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W), G.Connected → H.Connected → pebblingNumber (G □ H) ≤ pebblingNumber G * pebblingNumber H

name: Pebbling Number of a Path
msc: 05C05 Trees; 05C69 Dominating sets, independent sets, cliques
informal_statement_summary: A legal pebbling move removes two pebbles from a vertex and places one at an adjacent vertex. The pebbling number is the least size for which every configuration can reach every prescribed root by finitely many legal moves. For the path on n + 1 vertices, this number is exactly 2^n, for all n ≥ 0. This classical solved problem is an elementary calibration task reusing P082's definitions.
formal_statement: theorem P083 (n : ℕ) : pebblingNumber (pathGraph (n + 1)) = 2 ^ n

name: Cayley's Formula via Prüfer Codes
msc: 05C05 Trees; 05A19 Combinatorial identities, bijective combinatorics
informal_statement:
\section*{Challenge 84: Cayley's Formula via Prüfer Codes}
\refstepcounter{section}

Let $\mathcal{T}_n$ be the set of simple connected acyclic graphs on the fixed vertex set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. These are unrooted labelled trees: labels are distinguished, and we do not identify isomorphic graphs.

\begin{theorem}[Cayley's formula]
For $n\geq2$, $|\mathcal{T}_n|=n^{n-2}$. There is exactly one tree on a single vertex.
\end{theorem}

The formal statement combines the two cases as $|\mathcal{T}_n|=n^{n-2}$ for $n\geq1$, using natural subtraction, so its right side at $n=1$ is $1^0=1$.

The complete solution uses Prüfer codes, sequences of length $n-2$ with entries in the vertex set. Repeatedly delete the least-labelled leaf and record its unique neighbour until two vertices remain. The decoder joins the least remaining label absent from the current code to the first entry, removes that label and entry, and finally joins the two remaining labels. The two procedures are inverse, giving
\[
\mathcal{T}_n\simeq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^{\{0,\ldots,n-3\}}.
\]
The exponent set here has size $n-2$ and is empty when $n=2$.

See \cite{GraphTheoryNotesPrufer}. The statement follows the ProofAtlas formalisation \cite{ProofAtlas2026Cayley}. It retains the actual encoder and decoder, not an arbitrary equivalence extracted from a cardinality theorem.

\begin{thebibliography}{2}
\bibitem{GraphTheoryNotesPrufer} \emph{Graph Theory Notes}, Section 3.1: Prüfer Codes. \url{https://ptwiddle.github.io/Graph-Theory-Notes/s_graphalgorithms_prufer.html}.
\bibitem{ProofAtlas2026Cayley} Advameg, Inc. \emph{Cayley's Formula for Labeled Trees: Lean Formalization}. ProofAtlas (2026). \url{https://www.proofatlas.ai/sources/cayley-tree-formula/}.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: For n ≥ 2, there are exactly n^(n-2) unrooted labelled trees on the fixed vertex set {0,…,n-1}; for n = 1 there is one. Trees are finite simple connected acyclic graphs, not graph-isomorphism classes. The complete solution constructs the classical Prüfer encoding, proves its decoder is inverse, and counts the length-n-2 codes. It is an elementary solved calibration problem. The public statement uses only mathlib's SimpleGraph.IsTree and Nat.card; all encoding and solution machinery is private.
formal_statement: theorem P084 (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) : Nat.card {G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) // G.IsTree} = n ^ (n - 2)

name: Lonely Runner Conjecture (Integer Speeds)
msc: 11K60 Diophantine approximation; 11J13 Simultaneous homogeneous approximation, linear forms
informal_statement_summary: For any k ≥ 1 nonzero integer speeds v₁,…,v_k, there is a real time t such that every t vᵢ is at distance at least 1/(k+1) from the nearest integer. This is the stationary-runner integer formulation: k speeds correspond to k+1 runners. Negative and repeated speeds are allowed. The full conjecture remains open; recent preprints report computer-assisted proofs through fourteen runners, not a general solution.
formal_statement: theorem P085 (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k) (v : Fin k → ℤ) (hv : ∀ i, v i ≠ 0) : ∃ t : ℝ, ∀ i, (1 : ℝ) / (k + 1) ≤ ‖((t * v i : ℝ) : UnitAddCircle)‖

name: Rainbow Trees in Subgraphs of Hypercubes
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 05C05 Trees
informal_statement_summary: Let G be a nonempty finite simple graph isomorphic to a (not necessarily induced) subgraph of an n-dimensional hypercube. Give its edges a proper colouring: edges sharing a vertex have distinct colours. Then every finite tree T with at most δ(G) edges has a rainbow copy in G, meaning an injective edge-preserving vertex map under which distinct edges of T receive distinct colours. Here δ(G) is the minimum degree. This is Theorem 1.2 of Crawford–Sankar–Schildkraut–Spiro, Rainbow Trees in Hypercubes (2025). In particular, every proper edge-colouring of Q_n contains every tree with at most n edges as a rainbow copy. P014 concerns the absence of rainbow cycles in the coordinate colouring; this is a different result.
formal_statement: theorem P086 {V W C : Type*} [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] [Fintype W] (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (ι : G →g H n) (hι : Injective ι) (c : G.lineGraph.Coloring C) (T : SimpleGraph W) [DecidableRel T.Adj] (hT : T.IsTree) (hsize : T.edgeFinset.card ≤ G.minDegree) : ∃ f : T →g G, Injective f ∧ Injective (c ∘ f.mapEdgeSet)

name: Galvin's Bipartite List-Edge-Colouring Theorem
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs
informal_statement_summary: Let M be a finite loopless bipartite multigraph, with parallel edges retained as distinct edge objects. Suppose every vertex is incident with at most d edges. For each edge e, choose a finite list L(e) of at least d allowed colours from an arbitrary common palette. Galvin's theorem asserts that one can select a colour c(e) from every list so that any two distinct edges with a common endpoint have different colours. No positivity condition on d is needed: the empty-edge case is included. The formal statement uses two-colourability of the underlying simple graph for bipartiteness, an explicit loop exclusion, and injectivity on incident edge sets for properness. This is a proved theorem and an upper-end calibration target, not an open list-colouring conjecture. A proven reduction derives Dinitz's theorem on choosing representatives from an n-by-n array of lists, distinct in each row and column.
formal_statement: theorem P087 {V E C : Type*} [Finite V] [Fintype E] [DecidableEq V] (d : ℕ) (M : Multigraph V E) (hloop : ∀ e, ¬M.IsLoop e) (hbi : M.toSimpleGraph.Colorable 2) (hdegree : ∀ v, (M.incidenceFinset v).card ≤ d) (L : E → Finset C) (hL : ∀ e, d ≤ (L e).card) : ∃ c : E → C, (∀ e, c e ∈ L e) ∧ ∀ v, Set.InjOn c ↑(M.incidenceFinset v)

name: Elementary Ramsey Binomial Bound
msc: 05C55 Generalized Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: For positive integers r and s, every finite simple graph with at least choose(r+s−2,r−1) vertices contains a clique of size r or an independent set of size s. This is the classical Erdős–Szekeres binomial upper bound for two-colour Ramsey numbers, not P003's modern exponential improvement.
formal_statement: theorem P088 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (r s : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r) (hs : 1 ≤ s) (h : (r + s - 2).choose (r - 1) ≤ Fintype.card V) : (∃ t : Finset V, G.IsNClique r t) ∨ ∃ t : Finset V, Gᶜ.IsNClique s t

name: Erdős–Szekeres Monotone Subsequence Theorem
msc: 05D10 Ramsey theory; 06A05 Total order
informal_statement_summary: For positive integers r and s, any sequence of n distinct elements of a linear order with n > (r−1)(s−1) has a strictly increasing subsequence of length r or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length s. Subsequences preserve the original index order and need not be contiguous. This is the classical Erdős–Szekeres theorem, stated over an arbitrary linear order rather than only the real numbers. A complete reference Lean proof assigns each position the lengths of its longest increasing and decreasing subsequences and applies the pigeonhole principle. The central benchmark keeps its exercise placeholder; the independent solution is provided separately as an elementary calibration reference.
formal_statement: theorem P089 {α : Type*} [LinearOrder α] (r s n : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r) (hs : 1 ≤ s) (hn : (r - 1) * (s - 1) < n) (a : Fin n → α) (ha : Function.Injective a) : (∃ f : Fin r ↪o Fin n, StrictMono (a ∘ f)) ∨ ∃ f : Fin s ↪o Fin n, StrictAnti (a ∘ f)

name: Restricted Eigenvalues of Strongly Regular Graphs
msc: 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra (matrices, eigenvalues, etc.); 05E30 Association schemes, strongly regular graphs
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 90: Restricted eigenvalues of strongly regular graphs}
A finite simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is \emph{strongly regular} with
parameters $(n,k,\lambda,\mu)$ if it is $k$-regular, any two adjacent vertices
have exactly $\lambda$ common neighbours, and any two distinct non-adjacent
vertices have exactly $\mu$ common neighbours. Let $A$ be its adjacency matrix
over $\mathbb R$.
\begin{theorem}
If $Av=xv$ for a nonzero vector $v\in\mathbb R^{V(G)}$ whose coordinates sum to
zero, then
\[
x^2+(\mu-\lambda)x+(\mu-k)=0.
\]
\end{theorem}
Hence the eigenvalues of $A$ other than $k$ are the roots
$\tfrac12\bigl(\lambda-\mu\pm\sqrt{(\lambda-\mu)^2+4(k-\mu)}\bigr)$
\cite{Bose1963StronglyRegular,BrouwerHaemers2012Spectra,GodsilRoyle2001AGT}.

The formal statement uses Mathlib's \texttt{IsSRGWith} (with $\ell$ for
$\lambda$) and \texttt{adjMatrix}. The eigenvector is an arbitrary nonzero real
vector orthogonal to the all-ones vector, so no spectral theorem is needed.

\begin{thebibliography}{3}
\bibitem{Bose1963StronglyRegular}
R. C. Bose. \emph{Strongly regular graphs, partial geometries and partially
balanced designs}. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 13 (1963), 389--419.
\bibitem{BrouwerHaemers2012Spectra}
A. E. Brouwer, W. H. Haemers. \emph{Spectra of Graphs}. Universitext,
Springer, New York, 2012.
\bibitem{GodsilRoyle2001AGT}
C. Godsil, G. Royle. \emph{Algebraic Graph Theory}. Graduate Texts in
Mathematics 207, Springer, New York, 2001.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: A strongly regular graph with parameters (n, k, λ, μ) is k-regular on n vertices, with exactly λ common neighbours for adjacent pairs and μ for distinct non-adjacent pairs. Let A be its real adjacency matrix. If Av = xv for a nonzero vector v whose coordinates sum to zero, then x² + (μ − λ)x + (μ − k) = 0, so the eigenvalues other than k are the two roots of this quadratic. This is a classical calibration problem in algebraic graph theory. The formal statement uses Mathlib's IsSRGWith and adjMatrix with an arbitrary eigenvector orthogonal to the all-ones vector, so no spectral theorem is needed.
formal_statement: theorem P090 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {n k ℓ μ : ℕ} (hG : G.IsSRGWith n k ℓ μ) (x : ℝ) (v : V → ℝ) (hv : v ≠ 0) (hsum : ∑ i, v i = 0) (hx : G.adjMatrix ℝ *ᵥ v = x • v) : x ^ 2 + ((μ : ℝ) - ℓ) * x + ((μ : ℝ) - k) = 0

name: Bollobás's Uniform Set-Pairs Inequality
msc: 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 91: Bollobás's uniform set-pairs inequality}
Let $I$ be a finite index set, let $r,s\geq 0$, and let $A_i,B_i$ be finite
subsets of an arbitrary common universe, for $i\in I$.
\begin{theorem}[Bollobás]
If $|A_i|=r$, $|B_i|=s$ and $A_i\cap B_i=\varnothing$ for every $i$, and
$A_i\cap B_j\ne\varnothing$ for every ordered pair of distinct indices $i,j$,
then
\[
|I|\leq \binom{r+s}{r}.
\]
\end{theorem}
The cross-intersection condition is imposed in both directions, not just
for $i<j$. No assumption says that the unions $A_i\cup B_i$ coincide.
Only the index type is required to be finite in Lean; each individual set
is represented by a \texttt{Finset}. Disjointness expresses empty intersection,
and its negation expresses nonempty intersection without a decidable-equality
assumption in the public interface.

The bound is attained by all pairs $(A,X\setminus A)$ where $|X|=r+s$ and $|A|=r$.
If either size is zero, there can be at most one indexed pair. An empty family
is allowed.

\begin{thebibliography}{2}
\bibitem{Bollobas1965GeneralizedGraphs}
B. Bollobás. \emph{On generalized graphs}. Acta Mathematica Academiae
Scientiarum Hungaricae 16 (1965), 447--452.
\bibitem{Alon1985ExtremalSets}
N. Alon. \emph{An extremal problem for sets with applications to graph theory}.
Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 40 (1985), 82--89.
Corollary 1.2 with one ground part is the two-sided set-pairs theorem,
attributed there to Bollobás.
\end{thebibliography}
informal_statement_summary: Let (A_i,B_i) be a finite indexed family of pairs of finite sets, with every A_i having r elements and every B_i having s elements. Suppose A_i and B_i are disjoint, whereas A_i and B_j intersect whenever i≠j. Then there are at most choose(r+s,r) pairs. The ambient universe is arbitrary and need not have r+s elements; different pairs may have different unions. The empty family and zero sizes are included. Complementary pairs on a fixed (r+s)-element set attain the bound. A complete reference Lean proof establishes the stronger weighted set-pairs inequality by finite induction, implementing the first-element recurrence behind the permutation-events proof without measure theory.
formal_statement: theorem P091 {ι α : Type*} [Fintype ι] (r s : ℕ) (A B : ι → Finset α) (hA : ∀ i, (A i).card = r) (hB : ∀ i, (B i).card = s) (hdis : ∀ i, Disjoint (A i) (B i)) (hcross : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → ¬ Disjoint (A i) (B j)) : Fintype.card ι ≤ (r + s).choose r

name: Friendship Theorem (Erdős–Rényi–Sós)
msc: 05C75 Structural characterization of families of graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: In a nonempty finite simple graph, suppose every pair of distinct vertices has exactly one common neighbour, whether or not the pair is adjacent. Then there is a vertex adjacent to every other vertex. Equivalently, the graph consists of triangles sharing a common central vertex; the singleton graph is included as the degenerate case with no triangles. This is the proved friendship theorem of Erdős, Rényi and Sós (1966).
formal_statement: theorem P092 {V : Type*} [Finite V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (h : ∀ u v, u ≠ v → ∃! w, G.Adj u w ∧ G.Adj v w) : ∃ c, ∀ v, v ≠ c → G.Adj c v

name: Dirac's Hamiltonian-Cycle Theorem
msc: 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: A finite simple graph G with n >= 3 vertices has a Hamiltonian cycle if 2 deg(v) >= n for every vertex v. The statement uses Mathlib's Hamiltonian predicate, whose singleton convention is excluded by n >= 3. This is Dirac's proved theorem (1952).
formal_statement: theorem P093 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hn : 3 ≤ Fintype.card V) (hdeg : ∀ v, Fintype.card V ≤ 2 * G.degree v) : G.IsHamiltonian

name: Lossless Vertex Expanders, Existence Form (Hsieh–Lubotzky–Mohanty–Reiner–Zhang, Theorem 2.2)
difficulty: Research (existence form of HLMRZ Theorem 2.2; the paper's algorithmic clause is not asserted)
msc: 05C48 Expander graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 2.2 of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner and Zhang (2025): for every eps in (0,1] there is k = k(eps) such that for every beta in (0,1] there is d_0 with the following property: for all dL, dR >= d_0 with beta <= dL/dR <= beta + eps there is an infinite family of (k dL, k dR)-biregular bipartite graphs on Theta(n) vertices that are two-sided (1 - eps)-vertex expanders, i.e. for some eta > 0 every set S of vertices on one side with |S| <= eta times that side has at least (1 - eps) times (degree times |S|) neighbours. The paper's polynomial-time construction clause is not asserted; only existence is. Existence alone (even with k = 1 and without the ratio window) also follows from the probabilistic method, so the formal problem is the existence statement in the parameter form of Theorem 2.2, not the paper's explicit construction.
formal_statement: theorem P094 {eps : ℝ} (heps0 : 0 < eps) (heps1 : eps ≤ 1) : ∃ k : ℕ, 0 < k ∧ ∀ beta : ℝ, 0 < beta → beta ≤ 1 → ∃ d₀ : ℕ, 0 < d₀ ∧ ∀ dL dR : ℕ, d₀ ≤ dL → d₀ ≤ dR → beta * (dR : ℝ) ≤ (dL : ℝ) → (dL : ℝ) ≤ (beta + eps) * (dR : ℝ) → ∃ Z : ℕ → BipartiteGraph, (∀ n, (Z n).IsBiregular (k * dL) (k * dR)) ∧ HasThetaNVertices Z ∧ IsTwoSidedVertexExpanderFamily Z (k * dL) (k * dR) (1 - eps)

name: Explicit Two-Sided Unique-Neighbour Expanders (Hsieh–McKenzie–Mohanty–Paredes, Theorem 4.4)
msc: 05C48 Expander graphs; 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 4.4 of Hsieh, McKenzie, Mohanty and Paredes (2023): for every beta in (0, 1/2] there are d_0 and delta > 0 such that for all even d_1 <= d_2 with d_1, d_2 >= d_0 and beta d_2 <= (1 - beta) d_1 there are arbitrarily large N and bipartite graphs on N vertices, with degree 2 d_1 on one side and 2 d_2 on the other, in which every nonempty vertex set S with |S| <= N / d_1^3 has at least delta d_1 |S| unique neighbours (vertices adjacent to exactly one member of S). The strong explicitness and the Cayley-group refinement of the paper are not asserted.
formal_statement: theorem P095 {β : ℝ} (hβ0 : 0 < β) (hβ1 : β ≤ 1 / 2) : ∃ d₀ : ℕ, 0 < d₀ ∧ ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ d₁ d₂ : ℕ, d₀ ≤ d₁ → d₀ ≤ d₂ → Even d₁ → Even d₂ → d₁ ≤ d₂ → β * (d₂ : ℝ) ≤ (1 - β) * (d₁ : ℝ) → ∀ n₀ : ℕ, ∃ N : ℕ, n₀ ≤ N ∧ ∃ Z : SimpleGraph (Fin N), ∃ side : Fin N → Bool, (∀ u v : Fin N, Z.Adj u v → side u ≠ side v) ∧ (∀ v : Fin N, side v = true → Z.degree v = 2 * d₁) ∧ (∀ v : Fin N, side v = false → Z.degree v = 2 * d₂) ∧ HasExpansionProfileAtLeast (fun v => Z.neighborFinset v) (N / d₁ ^ 3) (δ * (d₁ : ℝ))

name: Characteristic and Matching Polynomials of a Uniform Hypertree (Li–Su–Fallat, Theorem 4.10)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C31 Graph polynomials; 15A69 Multilinear algebra, tensor calculus
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 4.10 of Li, Su and Fallat (2023): for an r-uniform hypertree T with at least one edge with m edges (r >= 2), the characteristic polynomial of its adjacency tensor factors as phi_T = prod over connected subgraphs H of T of phi_H^{a_H}, where phi_H is the matching polynomial of H, a_H = b^{m - e(H) - |bd(H)|} c^{e(H)} (b - c)^{|bd(H)|}, b = (r-1)^{r-1}, c = r^{r-2}, and bd(H) is the set of edges of T meeting H but not in H; single vertices contribute the factor lambda with boundary the star of the vertex. The characteristic polynomial is defined concretely through the Macaulay determinant formula as the polynomial quotient of two explicit matrix characteristic polynomials.
formal_statement: theorem P096 {r : ℕ} (hr : 2 ≤ r) {E : EdgeSet} (hT : IsRTree r E) : charPoly r E = (∏ v ∈ vertices E, (Polynomial.X : Polynomial ℤ) ^ aExp r E.card 0 (degree E v)) * ∏ F ∈ connectedSubgraphs E, matchingPoly r F ^ aExp r E.card F.card (boundary E F).card

name: Algebraic Connectivity of Token Graphs with a Cut Clique (Song–Dalfó–Fiol–Zhang, Theorem 5.3)
msc: 05C50 Graphs and linear algebra; 05C76 Graph operations
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 5.3 of Song, Dalfo, Fiol and Zhang (2024): let G be a graph on n vertices containing a clique K_r (r >= 1) each of whose vertices is adjacent to every vertex outside it, so that the clique has the maximum possible degree r(n - r), and whose removal disconnects G. Then for every 1 <= k <= n - 1 the algebraic connectivity (second smallest Laplacian eigenvalue) of G and of its k-token graph F_k(G) both equal r. For r = 1 this is the theorem of Barik and Verma on cut vertices of degree n - 1. Distinct from P069, which is the general spectral-gap equality alpha(F_k(G)) = alpha(G).
formal_statement: theorem P097 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] {r : ℕ} (hr : 1 ≤ r) (S : Finset V) (hcard : S.card = r) (hclique : G.IsClique (S : Set V)) (hdeg : ∀ u ∈ S, ∀ v ∉ S, G.Adj u v) (hcut : ¬ (G.induce ((S : Set V)ᶜ)).Preconnected) {k : ℕ} (hk1 : 1 ≤ k) (hk2 : k < Fintype.card V) : algConnectivity G = r ∧ algConnectivity (tokenGraph G k) = r

name: Mantel's Theorem
msc: 05C35 Extremal problems in graph theory
informal_statement_summary: Every triangle-free finite simple graph on n vertices has at most floor(n^2/4) edges. Triangle-free means that the complete graph on three vertices has no graph embedding into G. Empty and singleton graphs are allowed. It is the triangle case of Turán's theorem.
formal_statement: theorem P098 {htf : triangle_free G} : Finset.card (G.edgeSet.toFinset) ≤ (Fintype.card V)^2 / 4

name: Colouring the 1-Skeleton of d-Dimensional Triangulations (Planken, Theorem 1)
msc: 05C15 Coloring of graphs and hypergraphs; 57Q15 Triangulating manifolds
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1 of Planken (2024): for d >= 2 and a triangulation C of the d-sphere, the 1-skeleton of C has a proper (d+2)-colouring if and only if C has a subdivision in which the number of (d-1)-cells incident with every (d-2)-cell is divisible by three; for d = 3 both are equivalent to the maximal subdivision of C (every chamber subdivided) having a 2-edge-colouring without monochromatic 2-cells. A triangulation is a finite family of (d+1)-element chambers on natural-number vertices whose barycentric realisation is homeomorphic to the d-sphere and whose vertex links are combinatorial (d-1)-spheres (defined recursively in the same way, so that the triangulation is piecewise linear, as in the source); subdivisions replace a chamber by the d+1 chambers through a new vertex.
formal_statement: theorem P099 (d : ℕ) (_hd : 2 ≤ d) (C : Triangulation d) : (C.skeleton.Colorable (d + 2) ↔ C.Subdividable) ∧ (d = 3 → (C.skeleton.Colorable (d + 2) ↔ C.MaximalSubdivisionBichromatic))

name: The Tutte Decomposition of 2-Connected Graphs (Bourneuf–Planken, Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C40 Connectivity; 05C85 Graph algorithms
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Bourneuf and Planken (2025), the structural output of their linear-time algorithm: every 2-connected finite graph has a tree-decomposition of adhesion two, whose torsos (the triconnected components) are 3-connected graphs, cycles or K_2, such that the separations induced by the edges of the decomposition tree are exactly the totally nested 2-separations of the graph. The running-time bound, a statement about the word-RAM model, is not asserted.
formal_statement: theorem P100 {V : Type u} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (_hG : IsKConnected G 2) : ∃ (W : Type u) (D : TreeDecomp G W), (∀ t t' : W, D.tree.Adj t t' → (D.adhesion t t').card = 2) ∧ (∀ t : W, IsTutteTorso (D.torso t)) ∧ (∀ t t' : W, D.tree.Adj t t' → ∃ s : Separation G, s.order = 2 ∧ s.TotallyNested ∧ D.Induces t t' s) ∧ (∀ s : Separation G, s.order = 2 → s.TotallyNested → ∃ t t' : W, D.tree.Adj t t' ∧ D.Induces t t' s)

name: Upper Clique Transversals via Dual Conformality (Boros–Gurvich–Milanič–Uno, Theorem 4.1)
msc: 05C65 Hypergraphs; 05C69 Vertex subsets with special properties
informal_statement_summary: The decision rule of Theorem 4.1 of Boros, Gurvich, Milanic and Uno: for k >= 2 and a finite graph G, let H be the hypergraph whose hyperedges are the minimal clique transversals of G of size less than k. Then the upper clique transversal number of G is at least k (G is a yes-instance of k-Upper Clique Transversal) exactly when H is not dually conformal or G differs from the co-occurrence graph of the dual hypergraph H^d. The paper's running-time estimate O(|V|^(3k-3)) for evaluating this rule is not asserted.
formal_statement: theorem P101 (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) (hk : 2 ≤ k) : HasLargeMinimalCliqueTransversal G k ↔ ¬ (DuallyConformal (smallMinimalCliqueTransversals G k) ∧ cooccurrenceGraph (dual (smallMinimalCliqueTransversals G k)) = G)

name: The Full Rank Condition for Sparse Random Matrices (Coja-Oghlan et al., Theorem 1.1)
msc: 60B20 Random matrices (probabilistic aspects); 15B52 Random matrices (algebraic aspects)
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Coja-Oghlan, Gao, Hahn-Klimroth, Lee, Muller and Rolvien (2021): let d and k >= 3 be degree laws with finite (2+eta)-th moments, let the gcd of the support of d be coprime to the field order q, and let chi be a law on the nonzero field elements; if Phi(z) < Phi(0) for all 0 < z <= 1 (the full rank condition (1.3)), then the random sparse matrix A_n(d, k, chi) over F_q, with independent nonzero coefficients on the edges of a uniformly random simple bipartite Tanner graph with the prescribed degrees, has full row rank with high probability as n tends to infinity along multiples of the check-degree gcd.
formal_statement: theorem P102 (F : Type*) [Field F] [Fintype F] (P : DegreeParameters) (χ : PMF F) (hχ : ∀ x ∈ χ.support, x ≠ 0) (η : Real) (hη : 0 < η) (hmoment_d : Summable fun r => P.variableDegree.mass r * (r : Real) ^ (2 + η)) (hmoment_k : Summable fun r => P.checkDegree.mass r * (r : Real) ^ (2 + η)) (kgcd : Nat) (hkgcd : P.checkDegree.IsSupportGCD kgcd) (hcoprime : FieldOrderCoprime F P) (hphi : P.StrictPhiCondition) : AsymptoticallyAlmostSurely fun t => fullRowRankProbability (randomMatrixLaw F P χ (kgcd * t)).toMeasure

name: The Dimension of Co-Sparse Random Bipartite Graph Orders (Gao–Kumar, Theorem 9)
msc: 06A07 Combinatorics of partially ordered sets; 05C80 Random graphs

name: Perfect Matchings in the Semi-Random Graph Process (Gao–MacRury–Prałat, Theorem 1.1)
msc: 05C80 Random graphs; 05C70 Edge subsets with special properties (matchings)
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Gao, MacRury and Pralat (2021): in the semi-random graph process, where in each round a vertex u_t is offered uniformly at random and the player chooses a vertex v_t and adds the edge u_t v_t, the perfect-matching threshold tau_PM satisfies tau_PM <= 1.20524: for every q < 1 and epsilon > 0 and all large n, some strategy builds a perfect matching on [n] (all but one vertex saturated when n is odd) with probability at least q within (1.20524 + epsilon) n rounds.
formal_statement: theorem P105 : tau perfectMatchingProperty ≤ 1.20524

msc: 05C80 Random graphs; 05C40 Connectivity
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Gao and Koerts (2023): for every fixed k >= 1 there is a real alpha_k such that for every epsilon > 0, (a) no strategy in the post-positional semi-random process (the offered vertex is revealed before the player's choice) or in the pre-positional process (the player chooses first) builds a k-connected graph within (alpha_k - epsilon) n rounds asymptotically almost surely, and (b) strategies in both processes build a k-connected graph within (alpha_k + epsilon) n rounds asymptotically almost surely. msc: 05C80 Random graphs; 05C45 Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs
informal_statement_summary: Theorem 1.1 of Frieze, Gao, MacRury, Pralat and Sorkin (2023): the Hamiltonian-cycle constant of the semi-random graph process satisfies C_HAM <= 1.81701: for every q < 1 and epsilon > 0 and all large n, some online strategy builds a Hamiltonian cycle on [n] with probability at least q within (1.81701 + epsilon) n rounds. The constant is the numerical solution of the paper's differential equations for the DegreeGreedy, FullyRandomized and clean-up phases.

name: Two Vertices of Equal Degree
msc: 05C07 Vertex degrees
informal_statement_summary: In any finite simple graph with at least two vertices, two distinct vertices have the same degree. Degrees lie between 0 and n-1, and a vertex of degree n-1 rules out a vertex of degree 0, so the n degrees take at most n-1 values and two coincide by the pigeonhole principle. A standard textbook exercise; the formal statement uses Mathlib's SimpleGraph and degree on a finite vertex type.
formal_statement: theorem P109 {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (h : 2 ≤ Fintype.card V) : ∃ u v, u ≠ v ∧ G.degree u = G.degree v

name: A Zero-Sum Block of Consecutive Integers
msc: 11B75 Other combinatorial number theory; 05D10 Ramsey theory
informal_statement_summary: Among any n ≥ 1 integers a_0, …, a_{n-1} some block of consecutive terms a_i + … + a_{j-1} (0 ≤ i < j ≤ n) is divisible by n. The n+1 prefix sums take at most n residues modulo n, so two agree and their difference is such a block. A classical exercise and a weak relative of the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv theorem (which Mathlib has in a different form). The formal statement uses a function ℕ → ℤ and a sum over Finset.Ico i j.
formal_statement: theorem P110 (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (a : ℕ → ℤ) : ∃ i j, i < j ∧ j ≤ n ∧ (n : ℤ) ∣ ∑ k ∈ Finset.Ico i j, a k

name: A Consecutive Pair Among n + 1 Numbers from [2n]
msc: 11B75 Other combinatorial number theory; 05D05 Extremal set theory
informal_statement_summary: Any n+1 integers chosen from {1, …, 2n} include two consecutive integers, hence two coprime ones. The n pairs {2k-1, 2k} cover {1, …, 2n}, so by the pigeonhole principle two of the n+1 numbers fall in the same pair. A classical exercise often attributed to Erdős. The formal statement takes a Finset S ⊆ Icc 1 (2n) with at least n+1 elements and asserts that a and a+1 both lie in S for some a.
formal_statement: theorem P111 (n : ℕ) (S : Finset ℕ) (hS : S ⊆ Icc 1 (2 * n)) (hcard : n + 1 ≤ S.card) : ∃ a ∈ S, a + 1 ∈ S

name: Matroid Intersection for Tame Matroids
msc: 05B35 Combinatorial aspects of matroids and geometric lattices
informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 112: Matroid intersection for tame matroids}
\refstepcounter{section}
Matroids may be infinite, in the sense of Bruhn, Diestel, Kriesell, Pendavingh and Wollan \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}: a matroid on a set $E$ is given by its independent sets, and every independent subset of any $X \subseteq E$ extends to a maximal independent subset of $X$. Circuits are the minimal dependent sets, cocircuits are the circuits of the dual matroid $M^*$, and $\mathrm{cl}_M$ denotes the closure operator of $M$.

\begin{definition}[Tame matroid]
A matroid $M$ is \emph{tame} if every circuit of $M$ meets every cocircuit of $M$ in finitely many elements.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Intersection property]
Matroids $M$ and $N$ on a common ground set $E$ \emph{satisfy intersection} if there is a set $J$ independent in both $M$ and $N$, and a partition $J = J_M \sqcup J_N$, such that
$$
\mathrm{cl}_M\ev{J_M} \cup \mathrm{cl}_N\ev{J_N} = E .
$$
\end{definition}

\begin{conjecture}[Matroid intersection for tame matroids]
Any two tame matroids on a common ground set satisfy intersection.
\end{conjecture}

For finite matroids the intersection property is equivalent to Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem. Nash-Williams conjectured it for pairs of finitary matroids (every circuit finite) \cite{AharoniZiv1998Intersection}; Bowler and Carmesin \cite{BowlerCarmesin2015Intersection} showed that for any two matroids $M$, $N$ the pair $(M,N)$ satisfies intersection if and only if $(M,N^*)$ admits a packing/covering partition, and formulated the unrestricted conjecture for all pairs of matroids. Known cases include pairs of finitary matroids on a countable ground set \cite{Joo2021Countable}, a nearly finitary matroid together with the dual of a nearly finitary matroid \cite{AignerHorevCarmesinFrohlich2018Intersection}, and pairs of tame matroids with a common decomposition by $2$-separations into finite parts \cite{BowlerCarmesin2015Intersection}; a proof claimed for all pairs of finitary matroids \cite{Alam2025Finitary} was withdrawn in January 2025, so the finitary case is open.

In October 2026 a counterexample to the unrestricted conjecture appeared \cite{OpenAI2026Matroid}: two partitional matroids on a countable ground set. Both are self-dual and have infinite circuits; in a self-dual matroid every circuit is also a cocircuit, so these matroids are not tame, and the conjecture for tame matroids remains open. Finitary and cofinitary matroids are tame, so the conjecture above contains Nash-Williams' original conjecture.

The formal statement uses Mathlib's \texttt{Matroid} (which follows the axioms of \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}), with \texttt{Matroid.Tame} and \texttt{Matroid.SatisfiesIntersection} defined in the ProofBench statement library.

\section*{Problem 113: Matroid intersection for tame matroids on a countable ground set}
\refstepcounter{section}
Matroids may be infinite, in the sense of Bruhn, Diestel, Kriesell, Pendavingh and Wollan \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}: a matroid on a set $E$ is given by its independent sets, and every independent subset of any $X \subseteq E$ extends to a maximal independent subset of $X$. Circuits are the minimal dependent sets, cocircuits are the circuits of the dual matroid $M^*$, and $\mathrm{cl}_M$ denotes the closure operator of $M$.

\begin{definition}[Tame matroid]
A matroid $M$ is \emph{tame} if every circuit of $M$ meets every cocircuit of $M$ in finitely many elements.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Intersection property]
Matroids $M$ and $N$ on a common ground set $E$ \emph{satisfy intersection} if there is a set $J$ independent in both $M$ and $N$, and a partition $J = J_M \sqcup J_N$, such that
$$
\mathrm{cl}_M\ev{J_M} \cup \mathrm{cl}_N\ev{J_N} = E .
$$
\end{definition}

\begin{conjecture}[Matroid intersection for tame matroids on a countable set]
Any two tame matroids on a common countable ground set satisfy intersection.
\end{conjecture}

This is the countable case of Problem 112. For finite matroids it is Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem. On countable ground sets it is known for two finitary matroids \cite{Joo2021Countable}, and for two matroids each of which is finitary or cofinitary: Jo\'o proved the packing/covering conjecture in that setting \cite{Joo2024PackingCovering}, and by Bowler and Carmesin \cite{BowlerCarmesin2015Intersection} the pair $(M,N)$ satisfies intersection if and only if $(M,N^*)$ admits a packing/covering partition.

In October 2026 a counterexample to the unrestricted conjecture appeared, on a countable ground set \cite{OpenAI2026Matroid}. Its two matroids are self-dual and have infinite circuits; in a self-dual matroid every circuit is also a cocircuit, so these matroids are not tame, and the countable tame case remains open.

The formal statement uses Mathlib's \texttt{Matroid} (which follows the axioms of \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}), with \texttt{Matroid.Tame} and \texttt{Matroid.SatisfiesIntersection} defined in the ProofBench statement library; countability is that of the ground set \texttt{M.E}.

\section*{Problem 114: Nash-Williams' matroid intersection conjecture}
\refstepcounter{section}
Matroids may be infinite, in the sense of Bruhn, Diestel, Kriesell, Pendavingh and Wollan \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}: a matroid on a set $E$ is given by its independent sets, and every independent subset of any $X \subseteq E$ extends to a maximal independent subset of $X$. A matroid is \emph{finitary} if a set is independent whenever all its finite subsets are; equivalently, all its circuits are finite. $\mathrm{cl}_M$ denotes the closure operator of $M$.

\begin{definition}[Intersection property]
Matroids $M$ and $N$ on a common ground set $E$ \emph{satisfy intersection} if there is a set $J$ independent in both $M$ and $N$, and a partition $J = J_M \sqcup J_N$, such that
$$
\mathrm{cl}_M\ev{J_M} \cup \mathrm{cl}_N\ev{J_N} = E .
$$
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nash-Williams' matroid intersection conjecture]
Any two finitary matroids on a common ground set satisfy intersection.
\end{theorem}

For finite matroids this is Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem. The conjecture is due to Nash-Williams; an early published formulation is in \cite{AharoniZiv1998Intersection}, which proves it when one of the matroids is a direct sum of countably many matroids of finite rank. Jo\'o proved it for countable ground sets \cite{Joo2021Countable}. Bowler and Carmesin \cite{BowlerCarmesin2015Intersection} showed that $(M,N)$ satisfies intersection if and only if $(M,N^*)$ admits a packing/covering partition. The conjecture implies the infinite Menger theorem of Aharoni and Berger \cite{AignerHorevCarmesinFrohlich2018Intersection}.

A proof for all pairs of finitary matroids, using nonstandard analysis, was claimed in 2025 \cite{Alam2025Finitary} and withdrawn the same month after a critical error was found; the general finitary case is open. The counterexample of October 2026 to the unrestricted conjecture \cite{OpenAI2026Matroid} is neither finitary nor cofinitary and does not bear on this statement. Finitary matroids are tame, so this problem is the finitary case of Problem 112.

The formal statement uses Mathlib's \texttt{Matroid} (which follows the axioms of \cite{BDKPW2013Axioms}) and its class \texttt{Matroid.Finitary}, with \texttt{Matroid.SatisfiesIntersection} defined in the ProofBench statement library.

\section*{The van der Waerden Conjecture}
\refstepcounter{section}

For $n\in\N_{>0}$, write
\[
[n] := \{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
and 
\[
[n]_0 := \{0,\ldots,n-1\}.
\]
Throughout, we use additive notation for the binary operation in a monoid. 

\begin{definition}[Homothetic copy]
Given a commutative monoid $M$, a subset $S\subseteq M$, an element $a\in M$ and a positive integer $d$, then $a+dS:= \{ a+ id : i\in S \}$ is called a \textit{homothetic copy} of $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Arithmetic progression]
\label{def:AP}
Let $m,d\in\N_{>0}$ and $a\in \N$. An \textit{$m$-term arithmetic progression}
in $\N$ is a set of the form
\[
A=\{a+id : i=0,\ldots,m-1\},
\]
The number $d$ is its
\textit{common difference}.
\end{definition}

Take $M:= \N$ and $a\in \N$. Fix positive integers $m,d\in \N^+$. Let  $S := [m]_0$, Then, the homothetic copy $a+dS$ is an $m$-term AP, with common difference $d$.



\begin{definition}
Given a commutative monoid $M$, and a coloring $M\to[r]$, then a subset $S\subseteq M$ is \textit{monochromatic}, provided there is some $i\in [r]$ such that $c\ev{S}=i$. 
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Filter, ultrafilter]
\label{def:filter}
Let $X$ be a set. A \textit{filter} on $X$ is a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $X$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(F1)] $X\in\mathcal F$ and $\emptyset\notin\mathcal F$;
\item[(F2)] if $A,B\in\mathcal F$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal F$;
\item[(F3)] if $A\in\mathcal F$ and $A\subseteq B\subseteq X$, then $B\in\mathcal F$.
\end{enumerate}
An \textit{ultrafilter} on $X$ is a filter $\mathcal U$ such that for every $A\subseteq X$, either $A$ or $X\setminus A$ lies in $\mathcal U$. %(Both cannot lie in $\mathcal U$: their intersection is $\emptyset$, so (F2) would contradict (F1).)
\end{definition}
In the literature, a family of subsets $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying the conditions (F1)-(F3) is sometimes called a ``proper'' filter, whereas a filter is taken as a family satisfying (F2)-(F3). Note that $ \emptyset \in \mathcal{F}$ if and only if $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{P}\ev{X}$.

\begin{definition}[Cofinite filter]
\label{ex:cofinite}
If $X$ is infinite, then $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{X}:=\{A\subseteq X : X\setminus A\text{ is finite}\}$ is a filter on $X$, the \textit{cofinite filter}, as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (F1) holds, since $X\setminus X=\emptyset$ is finite and in $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}$\ $X\setminus\emptyset=X$ is infinite.

\item (F2) holds as follows: Let $A,B \in \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}$ be given. Since $X\setminus A$ and $X\setminus B$ are finite sets, $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}$ 
then $X\setminus(A\cap B)=(X\setminus A)\cup(X\setminus B)$ is also finite, and so $ A \cap B \in \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{X}$.

\item (F3) holds as follows: Let $A \in \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{X}$ be given. Assume $A\subseteq B\subseteq X$  then $X\setminus B\subseteq X\setminus A$. Since  $X\setminus A$  finite  $X\setminus B$ is finite. Hence $B\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{X}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

Given $n\in \N$, let 
$\Gamma_n := \{N\in\N : N\geq n \}$. Note that $\Gamma_n \in \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{\N}$.

\begin{definition}
Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set (poset). 
\begin{enumerate}
\item An element $x\in P$ is a \textit{maximal} element if for any $y\in P$, if $x\leq y$ then $x=y$.
\item Given $x,y \in P$, $x$ and $y$ are comparable if $x\leq y$ or $y\leq x$. 
\item A \textit{chain} in $P$ is a subset $\mathcal C\subseteq P$ so that any pair of elements of $\mathcal{C}$ are comparable.
\end{enumerate}

\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Zorn's lemma]
if $P$ is nonempty and every nonempty chain in $P$ has an upper bound in $P$, then $P$ has a \textit{maximal element}. 
\end{lemma}
The proof of Zorn's lemma is skipped here. Zorn's lemma is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice over ZF.

\begin{lemma}[Ultrafilter lemma]
\label{lem:ultrafilter}
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal F$ be a filter on $X$. Then there is an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $X$ such that $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: extending a filter by one set.} Let $\mathcal G$ be a filter on $X$ and let $A\subseteq X$ with $X\setminus A\notin\mathcal G$. Define
\[
\mathcal G[A]:=\{B\subseteq X : A\cap C\subseteq B\text{ for some }C\in\mathcal G\}.
\]
Note that $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal G[A]$ (given $B\in\mathcal G$, take $C:=B$) and $A\in\mathcal G[A]$ (take $C:=X$). We claim that $\mathcal G[A]$ is a filter on $X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item (F1): $X\in\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal G[A]$. Assume for a contradiction that $\emptyset\in\mathcal G[A]$. Then $A\cap C\subseteq\emptyset$ for some $C\in\mathcal G$, i.e.\ $C\subseteq X\setminus A$, so $X\setminus A\in\mathcal G$ by (F3), contrary to assumption.
\item (F2): Let $D,E\in\mathcal G[A]$. By definition there are $C,C'\in\mathcal G$ with $A\cap C\subseteq D$ and $A\cap C'\subseteq E$. Hence
\[
A\cap(C\cap C')\subseteq D\cap E,
\]
and $C\cap C'\in\mathcal G$ by (F2) for $\mathcal G$. Therefore $D\cap E\in\mathcal G[A]$.
\item (F3): Let $D\in\mathcal G[A]$ and $D\subseteq E\subseteq X$. There is $C\in\mathcal G$ with $A\cap C\subseteq D\subseteq E$, hence $E\in\mathcal G[A]$.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Step 2: a maximal filter containing $\mathcal F$.} Let $P$ be the set of all filters $\mathcal G$ on $X$ with $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal G$, partially ordered by inclusion. Then $P\neq\emptyset$, since $\mathcal F\in P$. Let $\mathcal C\subseteq P$ be a nonempty chain and put $\mathcal G_\ast:=\bigcup\mathcal C$. Clearly $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal G_\ast$, and $\mathcal G_\ast$ is a filter on $X$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (F1): $X\in\mathcal G_\ast$ since $\mathcal C\neq\emptyset$, and $\emptyset\notin\mathcal G_\ast$ since $\emptyset$ lies in no member of $\mathcal C$.
\item (F2): Let $D,E\in\mathcal G_\ast$, say $D\in\mathcal G_1$ and $E\in\mathcal G_2$ with $\mathcal G_1,\mathcal G_2\in\mathcal C$. As $\mathcal C$ is a chain, we may assume $\mathcal G_1\subseteq\mathcal G_2$. Then $D,E\in\mathcal G_2$, so $D\cap E\in\mathcal G_2\subseteq\mathcal G_\ast$.
\item (F3): Let $D\in\mathcal G_\ast$, say $D\in\mathcal G_1\in\mathcal C$, and $D\subseteq E\subseteq X$. Then $E\in\mathcal G_1\subseteq\mathcal G_\ast$.
\end{enumerate}
So $\mathcal G_\ast\in P$ is an upper bound of $\mathcal C$. By Zorn's lemma, $P$ has a maximal element $\mathcal U$.

\emph{Step 3: $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter.} Let $A\subseteq X$ and suppose $X\setminus A\notin\mathcal U$. By Step 1, $\mathcal U[A]$ is a filter on $X$ with $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal U[A]$, so $\mathcal U[A]\in P$, and the maximality of $\mathcal U$ gives $\mathcal U[A]=\mathcal U$. Hence $A\in\mathcal U[A]=\mathcal U$. Thus for every $A\subseteq X$, either $X\setminus A\in\mathcal U$ or $A\in\mathcal U$, and $\mathcal U\supseteq\mathcal F$ is the required ultrafilter.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Ultrafilters and finite partitions]
\label{lem:partition}
Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on $X$, let $Y\in\mathcal U$, and let $Y=B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_r$ with $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ pairwise disjoint. Then exactly one of $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ lies in $\mathcal U$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At most one: if $B_i,B_j\in\mathcal U$ with $i\neq j$, then $\emptyset=B_i\cap B_j\in\mathcal U$ by (F2), contradicting (F1). At least one: otherwise $X\setminus B_i\in\mathcal U$ for every $i\in[r]$, as $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter, and $r$ applications of (F2) give
\[
Y\cap\bigcap_{i\in[r]}(X\setminus B_i)=Y\setminus\bigcup_{i\in[r]}B_i=\emptyset\in\mathcal U,
\]
again contradicting (F1).
\end{proof}
\begin{definition}[Hypercube and combinatorial lines]
For \(t,n\in\N^{+}\), the \emph{\(n\)-dimensional \(t\)-cube} is
\[
[t]^{[n]}:=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n):x_i\in[t]\text{ for every }i\in[n]\}.
\]
A subset $L$ of $[t]^{[n]}$ is a \textit{combinatorial line} if there
exists a nonempty set $I \subseteq [n]$ and integers $a_i$ for each $i \in I$ such that
$$
L = \{(x_1, . . . , x_n) \in [t]^{[n]} : x_i = a_i \text{ for } i \in I \text{ and } x_i = x_j \text{ for } i, j \in I \}
$$
The coordinates in \(I\) are called \emph{active}; the remaining
coordinates are \emph{fixed}.
\end{definition}

We collect some relevant theory below. 

\begin{enumerate}
%Overleaf-> References -> 0.Hales Jewett
\item \emph{Hales--Jewett theorem} \cite{HalesJewett1963}.
For every \(r,t\in\N^{+}\), there exists \(N\in\N^{+}\) such
that every coloring
$ c: [t]^{[N]}\longrightarrow[r]$ contains a monochromatic combinatorial line. 

\item \emph{Homothetic-copy theorem.}
Let \(M\) be a commutative monoid, let \(S\subseteq M\) be finite,
and let \(r\in\N^{+}\).
For every coloring \(c:M\to[r]\), there exist \(a\in M\) and
\(d\in\N_{>0}\) such that \(a+dS\) is monochromatic.
\item (van der Waerden theorem, infinite domain) For every \(r,m\in\N^{+}\), every coloring
$ c:\N\longrightarrow[r] $
contains a monochromatic \(m\)-term AP.

\item (van der Waerden theorem, finite domain) For every \(r,m\in\N^{+}\), there exists \(N\in\N^{+}\) such
that every coloring $c:[N]\longrightarrow[r] $ contains a monochromatic \(m\)-term AP.
% Theorem 1.2.8
% https://www.sfu.ca/~vjungic/v.pdf

\end{enumerate}
(1) $\to$ (2): 

\begin{proof}
Without loss of generality, $S$ is nonempty. Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_t\}\). By Hales-Jewett theorem, there is some $N$ such that any coloring $[t]^{[N]} \to [r] $ has a monochromatic combinatorial line. Define a coloring
\[
\widetilde c:[t]^{[N]}\longrightarrow[r],
\qquad
\widetilde c(x_1,\ldots,x_N)
=
c\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{x_i}\right).
\]
By the Hales--Jewett theorem, this coloring has a monochromatic
combinatorial line \(L\).
Let \(I\subseteq[N]\) be its nonempty set of active coordinates,
and let \(u_i\in[t]\) be the fixed value at coordinate \(i\notin I\).

Set
\[
a:=\sum_{i\in[N]\setminus I}s_{u_i},
\qquad
d:=|I|>0.
\]
For each \(j\in[t]\), the point of \(L\) whose active coordinates
all equal \(j\) is mapped by summation to
\[
\sum_{i\notin I}s_{u_i}+\sum_{i\in I}s_j
=
a+ds_j.
\]
Since \(L\) is monochromatic under \(\widetilde c\), all elements of
\[
a+dS=\{a+ds_j:j\in[t]\}
\]
have the same color under \(c\).
\end{proof}

This argument is already formalized in $\texttt{Combinatorics.exists\_mono\_homothetic\_copy}$

(2) $\to$ (3): We take $\N$ in the place of $M$; additionally we take $S:=[m]_0$ to obtain a monochromatic $m$-term AP.

(3) $\to$ (4):

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:ultrafilter} applied to the cofinite filter, there is an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $\N$ with $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cof}}\ev{\N}\subseteq\mathcal U$; in particular $\Gamma_n\in\mathcal U$ for every $n\in\N$.

Fix $r,m\in\N^{+}$ and suppose, for a contradiction, that no $N$ works: for every $N\in\N_{>0}$ there is a coloring $c_N:[N]\to[r]$ such that no $m$-term AP contained in $[N]$ is monochromatic under $c_N$. 

For $n\in\N_{>0}$ and $i\in[r]$ put
\[
B_{n,i}:=\{N\in\Gamma_n : c_N(n)=i\}.
\]
(For $N\in\Gamma_n$ we have $n\in[N]$, so $c_N(n)$ is defined.) For fixed $n$, the sets $B_{n,1},\ldots,B_{n,r}$ are pairwise disjoint with union $\Gamma_n\in\mathcal U$, so by \Cref{lem:partition} there is exactly one $i\in[r]$ with $B_{n,i}\in\mathcal U$; define $c(n):=i$. This yields a coloring $c:\N_{>0}\to[r]$ with
\[
B_{n,c(n)}\in\mathcal U\qquad\text{for every }n\in\N_{>0}.
\]

Apply (3) to the coloring $\N\to[r]$, $n\mapsto c(n+1)$: there is an $m$-term AP $\{a+id : i\in[m]_0\}\subseteq\N$ on which $n\mapsto c(n+1)$ is constant, say with value $j\in[r]$. Then
\[
A:=\{(a+1)+id : i\in[m]_0\}
\]
is an $m$-term AP in $\N_{>0}$ with $c(n)=j$ for every $n\in A$. Hence $B_{n,j}\in\mathcal U$ for every $n\in A$, and since $A$ is finite, $m-1$ applications of (F2) give
\[
B:=\bigcap_{n\in A}B_{n,j}\in\mathcal U,
\]
so $B\neq\emptyset$ by (F1). Pick $N\in B$. For every $n\in A$ we then have $N\in\Gamma_n$, i.e.\ $n\leq N$, and $c_N(n)=j$. Thus $A\subseteq[N]$ is a monochromatic $m$-term AP under $c_N$, contradicting the choice of $c_N$. Therefore some $N$ works, which is (4).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Van der Waerden number]
\label{def:vanDerWaerdenNumber}
Let $r,m\in\N_{>0}$. The \textit{van der Waerden number}
$W(r,m)$ is the least positive integer $N$ such that every coloring $ c:[N]\longrightarrow [r]$ contains a monochromatic $m$-term AP. This is well-defined by van der Waerden theorem.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
Given \(r,t\in\N^{+}\), the \textit{Hales-Jewett} number $HJ(r,t)$ is the least \(N\in\N^{+}\) such
that every coloring
$ c: [t]^{[N]}\longrightarrow[r]$ contains a monochromatic combinatorial line.
\end{definition}
%Exercise
\begin{proposition}
$$
W(1,m) = m
$$
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Part 1: $ m \leq W(1,m)$. 

It is enough to show that for any $N<m$, any $1$-coloring of $[N]$ is devoid of any monochromatic AP. Let $N < m$ be given. For any $1$-coloring of $[N]$, there is no AP in $[N]$, let alone monochromatic AP, because the lenght of largest AP is $[N]$ is $N$. 

Part 2: $ W(1,m) \leq m $. 

Given any $1$ - coloring of $[m]$, there exists a monochromatic AP, namely $ \{1,2,\ldots,m \} $, with common difference $1$. 
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Mixed van der Waerden number]
\label{def:mixedVanDerWaerdenNumber}
Let $k,\ell\in\N_{>0}$. The \textit{mixed van der Waerden number}
$w(k,\ell)$ is the least positive integer $n$ such that every
red-blue coloring of $[n]$ contains either a red $k$-term arithmetic
progression or a blue $\ell$-term arithmetic progression.
\end{definition}

These numbers exist by (4), and swapping the two colors shows $w(k,\ell)=w(\ell,k)$. In particular, $w(m,m)=W(2,m)$.

\begin{conjecture}[Concavity of mixed van der Waerden numbers]
\label{conj:vanderWaerdenConcavity}
For all $k,\ell\in\N$ satisfying $k\geq\ell\geq2$,
\[
w(k,\ell)\geq w(k+1,\ell-1).
\]
\end{conjecture}

Along each antidiagonal $k + \ell = s$ the conjecture says that $w$ does not increase as the pair $(k,\ell)$ becomes less balanced; with the symmetry, the numbers $w(s-\ell,\ell)$ are then largest at the middle of the antidiagonal. For example, $w(4,4) = 35$, $w(5,3) = 22$, $w(6,2) = 11$ and $w(7,1) = 7$. The conjecture was stated in 2000 and published in \cite{LandmanRobertson2003Ramsey} and \cite{KhodkarLandman2007Recent}; it is listed in the Open Problem Garden \cite{Landman2007OPGConcavity}. A direct computation confirms it for all pairs with $k + \ell \leq 9$.

The formal statement colours $\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ instead of $[n]$, which gives the same numbers, and requires $\ell \geq 2$, so that both numbers in the inequality have positive arguments. The numbers $w(k,\ell)$ are defined in the ProofBench statement library as \texttt{VanDerWaerden.mixedVdW}.

informal_statement:
\section*{Problem 116: Ramsey Numbers}
\refstepcounter{section}

\begin{definition}[Ramsey Number]
Given $t\in \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{(diagonal) Ramsey number} \( R(t) \) is the smallest $n\in \mathbb{N}\cup \{\infty\}$ such that every simple graph \( G \) on \( n \) vertices contains either a clique of size \( t \) or an independent set of size \( t \).
\end{definition}
By Ramsey's theorem, $R(t)$ is always an integer, which is upper bounded by $4^t$ \cite{ramsey1930formal, ramseygraham1990ramsey}.
Erd\H{o}s proved that random graphs $G(n,p)$ give a lower bound of the form $\sqrt{2}^t$ for $t$ sufficently large \cite{erdos1947some}. An important problem  that can be traced back to Ramsey's original paper \cite{ramsey1930formal} is to get good upper and lower bounds for the Ramsey number.

\begin{openproblem}[Scaled Ramsey problem]
Let $r\in \mathbb{N}$.
Provide decimal numbers $d_1$ and $d_2$ with $|d_2-d_1|\leq (4-\sqrt{2}) \cdot 0.96^r$ so that for all sufficiently large $t\in \mathbb{N}$
\[
d_1^t \leq R(t) \leq d_2^t.
\]
\end{openproblem}

The scaled Ramsey problem for $r=0$ follows by combining the above mentioned works of Ramsey and Erd\H{o}s.
With the bound $R(t) \leq 3.8^t$ of Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin and Wei \cite{gupta2024optimizing}, which sharpens the exponential improvement of Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe \cite{campos2026exponential}, the problem is solved for $r \leq 1$: the known bracket $[\sqrt{2}, 3.8]$ has width $3.8 - \sqrt{2} < 2.39 < (4 - \sqrt{2}) \cdot 0.96$. It is open from $r = 2$ onwards.

informal_statement_summary: The diagonal Ramsey number R(t) is the least n such that every simple graph on n vertices contains a clique of size t or an independent set of size t (equivalently, every 2-colouring of the edges of the complete graph K_n yields a monochromatic K_t). Ramsey's theorem gives R(t) ≤ 4^t, and Erdős's probabilistic argument gives R(t) ≥ (√2)^t for large t, so the exponential growth rate of R(t) lies between √2 and 4. The scaled Ramsey problem asks, for each r ∈ ℕ, for explicit real numbers d₁ ≤ d₂ with d₁^t ≤ R(t) ≤ d₂^t for all sufficiently large t and a controlled gap |d₂ − d₁| ≤ (4 − √2)·0.96^r; as r → ∞ the gap tends to 0, pinning down the growth rate exactly. The case r = 0 is the Ramsey–Erdős bound, and the case r = 1 follows from the exponential improvement of Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe together with the optimisation R(t) ≤ 3.8^t of Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin and Wei; the problem is open from r = 2 onwards.

informal_statement_summary: Let G be a finite simple graph. A proper edge-colouring of G assigns a colour to each edge so that any two edges sharing a common endpoint receive different colours, and Δ(G), the maximum degree of G, is the largest number of edges incident with any single vertex. Vizing's theorem states that G has a proper edge-colouring with Δ(G) + 1 colours. This challenge asks for a constructive proof, without the axiom of choice: in Lean, the proof may depend on propext and Quot.sound but not on Classical.choice. The graph is given on the vertices 0, …, n − 1 with decidable adjacency, so a proof amounts to an algorithm, such as the one of Misra and Gries (1992), which colours the edges one at a time, rotating a fan of edges at a vertex and swapping two colours along an alternating path where necessary.
